## Author's thesis (paraphrased from source)

Organisational Behavior is presented as an applied behavioural science whose object is "the behavior of people in organizations" examined at three levels — the individual, the group, and the organisation as a whole [AP] (Ch 1, "What Is Organizational Behavior?"). The book's organising premise is that effective management requires both technical mastery and "people skills" — motivation, leadership, decision-making, communication, organising work, dealing with politics, and developing employees and the organisation (Ch 1, "Management and Organizational Behavior"). The text frames management as "the process of planning, organizing, directing, and controlling the activities of employees in combination with other resources to accomplish organizational objectives" [V] (Ch 1, "What Is Management?"), and argues that this work draws on psychology, sociology, anthropology, economics, and political science but is distinguished by its focus on the *organisation* rather than the discipline (Ch 1, "What Is Organizational Behavior?").

A second load-bearing claim runs through the volume: that *individual differences*, perceptual processes, and learning histories systematically shape work behaviour, and that each carries implications for how employees are managed [AR] (Ch 2-4). Personality traits, cognitive complexity, locus of control, perceptual selectivity, attribution biases, and reinforcement schedules each generate distinct managerial implications.

A third load-bearing claim is that *organisations are open systems* that must align internal structure, culture, and processes with external environmental demands; structural form should fit environmental complexity and change, and culture helps the organisation adapt to and integrate with its external environment [AR] (Ch 15-16; Ch 15.5, "Corporate Cultures"). The mechanistic-versus-organic distinction recurs in both chapters (Ch 15.3, "Organizational Designs and Structures"; Ch 16.1, "Organizational Structures and Design").

A fourth load-bearing claim is that motivation, performance, and reward must be linked through *expectancy* and *equity* mechanisms — employees exert effort when they perceive that effort produces performance, performance produces valued outcomes, and outcomes are distributed fairly relative to peers [AR] (Ch 7.3, "Process Theories of Motivation"; Ch 8, "Performance Appraisal and Rewards").

## Part I: The nature of work, management, and organisational behaviour (Ch 1)

The chapter's opening Exploring Managerial Careers feature, "The Management Challenge at Apple and Google", contrasts the 600 Apple engineers who delivered iOS 10 within two years with the almost 6,000 Microsoft engineers whose Vista work took considerably longer [AE]. It relays a Bain & Company study finding Apple, Google and Netflix 40 per cent more productive than the average company [BT, Bain & Company], and rejects the hiring-pool explanation: Google has about the same share of star performers as other companies but groups them dynamically in the most business-critical roles, and Apple had no weak links [AE]. The feature names the most fundamental question in management: "How do you balance productivity while maintaining employee satisfaction and commitment?" [V] (Ch 1, "The Management Challenge at Apple and Google").

### Work as an activity that produces value for others

The book opens with a definition of work as "an activity that produces something of value for other people," broadening the wage-effort exchange to a social context [V] (Ch 1.1, "The Nature of Work"). Work serves four functions for individuals: economic (income), social (workplace relationships and friendships), status (occupation as a clue to community standing), and identity / self-esteem / self-actualisation [AP] (Ch 1.1, "Functions of Work"). Without these, "individuals often experience sensations of powerlessness, meaninglessness, and normlessness—a condition called alienation" [V] (Ch 1.1, "Functions of Work"). The text quotes Freud approvingly: "Work has a greater effect than any other technique of living in binding the individual more closely to reality" (Ch 1.1, "Functions of Work").

### Six contemporary challenges for managers

The text frames the workplace as in continuous change, identifying six challenges: international competition, new technologies, increased quality (TQM), employee motivation and commitment, managing a diverse workforce, and ethical behaviour [AP] (Ch 1.2, "The Changing Workplace"). The competitive-strength argument is grounded in a Global Competitive Index ranking the United States second (5.9) behind Switzerland (Ch 1.2, Table 1.1).

The section's Managing Change feature, "Siri Struggles to Keep Up with the Competition", draws on press sources [BT, Statt; Nellis; Mickle]. It holds that amid fast-paced technology change, staying one step ahead and being able to pivot quickly are two critical elements of successful leadership [BT]. Outperformed by Google Assistant and Amazon's Alexa, Apple made its third change in a year to the leadership of Siri, bringing in John Giannandrea, formerly Google's head of search and AI [BT, Statt]. His challenges are fitting into a new culture and company, finding a balance on how to innovate in the new role, and applying best practices from his previous one; his success turns on how quickly he can adapt [BT] (Ch 1.2, "Siri Struggles to Keep Up with the Competition").

The section's Ethics in Practice feature, "Papa John’s Founder under Fire", draws on press sources [BT, Jargon; Friedman; Kirsch; Valinsky]. It opens on the point that a manager's words and actions matter: founder and chairman John Schnatter used derogatory comments and racial slurs on a media-training call, admitted fault, and was forced to resign as chairman after the local NAACP branch called for it. The board removed him from marketing, publicity and pizza boxes, stating that "Papa John’s is not an individual" [V] [BT, Kirsch]. Shares rose on his resignation, adding $50 million to his net worth [BT, Valinsky]. The feature reads the episode as the company's values prevailing, with maintaining an ethical standard still an important value to Schnatter and the company [BT] (Ch 1.2, "Papa John’s Founder under Fire").

### Managerial responsibilities, levels, and required skill mixes

Mary Parker Follett's definition of management as "the art of getting things done through people" anchors the modern definition (Ch 1.3, "What Is Management?"). Managers' responsibilities sort into nine activities: long-range planning, controlling, environmental scanning, supervision, coordinating, customer relations and marketing, community relations, internal consulting, and monitoring products and services [AP] (Ch 1.3, "Managerial Responsibilities").

Management hierarchy has three levels — *executive*, *middle*, *first-line* — and three skill types: technical, human relations, and conceptual. As one rises in the hierarchy, conceptual skill demand increases and technical skill demand decreases; human-relations skill is required at every level [AP] (Ch 1.3, "Variations in Managerial Work"). Citing Fast Company's prediction, the text says the 21st-century manager will need the ability to think of new solutions, comfort with chaos, technological understanding, high emotional intelligence, and the ability to integrate people and technology (Ch 1.3, "The Twenty-First Century Manager").

### A model of organisational behaviour

The text proposes a five-block model: individuals and groups; tasks and technology; organisation design; organisational processes (leadership, communication, decision-making, power, politics); and management as the glue that holds them together [AP] (Ch 1.4, "Building Blocks of Organizations"). It distinguishes *micro*-OB (individual and group behaviour) from *macro*-OB or organisation theory (organisation-wide design and environment relations) and argues against keeping the two separate (Ch 1.4, "What Is Organizational Behavior?").

The book quotes Nadler and Tushman to justify the difficulty of the field: "Understanding one individual's behavior is challenging in and of itself; understanding a group that's made up of different individuals and comprehending the many relationships among those individuals is even more complex. Imagine, then, the mind-boggling complexity of a large organization made up of thousands of individuals and hundreds of groups with myriad relationships among these individuals and groups." [V] (Ch 1.4, "A Model of Organizational Behavior and Management").

## Part II: Individual differences, personality, and culture (Ch 2)

The chapter's opening Exploring Managerial Careers feature, "Building Back Trust on the Back End", draws on press sources [BT, Cohen; Koren]. With trust in big banks damaged by breaches and scandals, among them Wells Fargo's admission of opening nearly two million accounts without customers' permission, Cathie Mahon, chief executive of the National Federation of Community Development Credit Unions, set out to educate and empower low-income residents about financial resources and launched CU Impact, a platform for clearer balance information, more trustworthy auto-pay and more information at ATMs [BT, Cohen; Koren]. The feature credits "Her willingness to embrace technology and embrace differences of customers, employees, and the company structure overall" [V] as the key to the business's future success (Ch 2, "Building Back Trust on the Back End"). Ch 2.1 uses her example to show that personal characteristics can strongly influence behaviour [AR] (Ch 2.1, "Individual and Cultural Factors in Employee Performance").

### Mental and physical abilities

Performance is largely a function of ability and motivation, drawing on an early model the text cites approvingly [BT] (Ch 2.1, "Individual and Cultural Factors in Employee Performance"). *Cognitive complexity* — the capacity to acquire, sort, and integrate environmental information — is a central managerial trait. High-cognitive-complexity managers are better at handling complex situations, are more consultative, seek out and process more information, integrate discrepant information, consider more solutions, and use more complex decision strategies [AP] (Ch 2.2, "Mental Abilities").

Mental abilities, an individual's intellectual capabilities, are summarised in seven dimensions: verbal comprehension, word fluency, number aptitude, inductive reasoning, memory, spatial aptitude and perceptual speed [AP] (Ch 2.2, Table 2.1). Physical abilities divide into basic physical abilities (dynamic, trunk, static and explosive strength; extent and dynamic flexibility; gross body coordination; equilibrium; stamina) and psychomotor abilities (control precision, multilimb coordination, response orientation, rate control, manual dexterity, finger dexterity, arm-hand steadiness, reaction time and aiming) [AP] (Ch 2.2, Table 2.2).

### Six personality traits relevant to work behaviour

The text identifies six work-relevant traits: self-esteem, locus of control, introversion-extroversion, authoritarianism, dogmatism, and dependability [AP] (Ch 2.4, "Personality and Work Behavior"). Internals (those with internal locus of control) "(1) exhibit greater work motivation, (2) have stronger expectations that effort will lead to actual high job performance, (3) perform better on tasks requiring learning or problem-solving, (4) typically receive higher salaries and salary increases, and (5) exhibit less job-related anxiety than externals" [V] (Ch 2.4, "Locus of Control"). Authoritarians perform better under rigid supervision; non-authoritarians perform better under participative supervision (Ch 2.4, "Authoritarianism and Dogmatism"). Dogmatic managers "tend to make decisions quickly, based on only limited information and with a high degree of confidence in the correctness of their decisions" [V] (Ch 2.4, "Dogmatism").

The section's Managing Change feature, "Personality Clash: Design vs. Default", draws on a press source [BT, Pacelle] to show the role of personality in the demise of one of America's largest and oldest architectural firms. In 1969 Philip Johnson made John Burgee his sole partner to run the management side so he could focus on design ("Every design architect needs a Burgee" [V]). Burgee's personality suited the nuts-and-bolts work, but he felt only Johnson's name reached the press, pressed for successive renamings of the firm, and in 1988 sent a memo limiting which projects Johnson could initiate; Johnson would not give up control over design. The clash of Johnson's creative and Burgee's controlling personality ended with Burgee asking Johnson to leave; Burgee underestimated client reaction, lost key contracts and filed for bankruptcy [BT, Pacelle] (Ch 2.4, "Personality Clash: Design vs. Default").

### Argyris's basic incongruity thesis

Chris Argyris's thesis is that *traditional work organisations conflict with the developmental needs of healthy adults* [BT] (Ch 2.5, "Personality and Organization: A Basic Conflict?"). As people mature they become more active, independent, varied, deeply interested, longer-perspectived, and more self-aware; organisations in pursuit of efficiency assign minimal control, expect passivity and dependence, demand short-term horizons, and impose repetitive tasks. The conflict is strongest among mature employees in highly structured organisations doing fragmented mechanised work — that is, at lower hierarchical levels (Ch 2.5).

The section's Managing Change feature, "Integrating Employee and Organizational Goals at Kayak", draws on press sources [BT, Hawkes; Hickey]. Against the bleak picture of the incongruity thesis, it notes that many companies are trying to build a partnership in which the goals of both employee and company are realised, while selecting carefully for fit with their culture. Kayak hires not on technical skills but on being the smartest person somebody knows, puts employees first through work-life balance, and empowers them to prototype ideas, fail fast and try again; its CTO says there is "no grand design" [V]. In short, "the company aims to reduce the possibility of a basic incongruity developing between employee and organizational goals" [V] [BT, Hawkes; Hickey] (Ch 2.5, "Integrating Employee and Organizational Goals at Kayak").

### Values, ethics, and the work ethic

A *value* is "an enduring belief that a specific mode of conduct or end-state of existence is personally or socially preferable to an opposite or converse mode of conduct or end-state of existence" [V] (Ch 2.6, citing Rokeach). Rokeach's instrumental versus terminal values distinction is presented as a useful classification for managers (Ch 2.6, "Characteristics of Values"). Average annual hours worked are presented as a comparative measure of work ethic: South Korea 2,070, US 1,789, Japan 1,742, UK 1,676, France 1,472, Germany 1,288 [V] (Ch 2.6, Table 2.3, OECD data, accessed 2018).

### Cultural dimensions and Hofstede framing

The text adopts Hofstede's definition of culture as "the collective programming of the mind which distinguishes the members of one human group from another" [V] (Ch 2.7, "What Is Culture?"). Kluckhohn and Strodtbeck's six dimensions for distinguishing cultures are reproduced: views of humanity, of nature, of interpersonal relationships, of activity and achievement, of time, and of space (Ch 2.7, "Dimensions of Culture"). The text observes that "the Hispanic culture within the United States places a high value on groups compared to individuals and as a consequence takes a more collective approach to decision-making" [V] (Ch 2.7).

## Part III: Perception, attribution, and attitudes (Ch 3)

The chapter's opening Exploring Managerial Careers feature, "Personal Perceptions Affect Workplace Harmony", is an unsourced vignette [AE]. Chaz works extra hours and takes on extra assignments to speed his career; James, content to do his regular job, sees this as "kissing up" [V], resents it and treats Chaz poorly without thinking about why Chaz acts that way. Chaz tells their manager, Jerry, of pressures at home: his wife is expecting and they are saving. Jerry talks with him about ways to measure Chaz's extra effort, plans to revisit his raise at the annual review, and suggests Chaz talk with James, expecting that if James understood the reasons he would feel less jealous and less threatened [AE] (Ch 3, "Personal Perceptions Affect Workplace Harmony").

### Perceptual selectivity and social perception

*Perception* is "the process by which one screens, selects, organizes, and interprets stimuli to give them meaning" [V] (Ch 3.1, "The Perceptual Process"). It produces "a partial, personal construction in which certain objects, selected by the individual for a major role, are perceived in an individual manner" — every perceiver "is, as it were, to some degree a nonrepresentational artist" [V] (Ch 3.1, citing Kretch and associates).

The Dearborn and Simon study is treated as a classic illustration: executives from different departments reading the same case identified different problems as primary based on their functional background — sales executives saw sales problems, production executives saw production problems, and so on [BT] (Ch 3.1, "Organizational Role"). Likert's data on supervisor-subordinate perceptual gaps are cited: supervisors reported giving "sincere and thorough praise" 80 per cent of the time; subordinates reported receiving it 14 per cent of the time [V] (Ch 3.1, Table 3.1).

### Three barriers to accurate social perception

The text identifies *stereotyping*, *selective perception*, and *perceptual defense* as the three primary barriers (Ch 3.2). Perceptual defence operates by raising the recognition threshold for emotionally disturbing stimuli, eliciting substitute perceptions, and arousing emotional reactions even when stimuli are not consciously recognised (Ch 3.2, "Perceptual Defense"). Four mechanisms of perceptual defence are documented from a Haire and Grunes study of student responses to factory workers being described as "intelligent": denial, modification and distortion, change in perception, and recognition but refusal to change [BT] (Ch 3.2, "Perceptual Defense").

The section's Expanding Around the Globe feature, "To See Ourselves as Others See Us", uses Table 3.3 to show how visitors from seven countries stereotype the typical American [AP]. Its quotations, from Feig and Blair's *There Is a Difference* [BT, Feig; Blair], describe Americans as in a perpetual hurry (India), distant (Kenya), stopping at a stop sign with no traffic in sight (Turkey), treating life as only work (Colombia), analysing everything (Indonesia), and wanting an explicit yes or no (Ethiopia); an Iranian visitor was shocked when a professor said "I don’t know the answer, I will have to look it up" [V], where a professor at home would give a wrong answer rather than admit ignorance. The feature asks readers to weigh the accuracy of these perceptions and reassess their own stereotypes [AP] (Ch 3.2, Table 3.3).

### Attribution theory and bias

Attribution theory (Heider, Kelley) explains how individuals interpret events as caused by stable internal or external factors [BT] (Ch 3.3). Kelley's three factors — consensus, consistency, distinctiveness — combine to produce internal or external attribution: low consensus, high consistency, low distinctiveness yields internal attribution (skill); high consensus, high consistency, high distinctiveness yields external attribution (luck or task ease) (Ch 3.3, "Internal and External Causes of Behavior").

Two attribution biases are central to the OB analysis. The *fundamental attribution error* is "a tendency to underestimate the effects of external or situational causes of behavior and to overestimate the effects of internal or personal causes" [V] (Ch 3.3, "Attributional Bias"). The text draws the consequence: "Hence, when a major problem occurs within a certain department, we tend to blame people rather than events or situations" [V] (Ch 3.3, "Attributional Bias"). The *self-serving bias* is the tendency to attribute success to one's own actions and failure to others (Ch 3.3, "Attributional Bias"). "These two biases in interpreting how we see the events around us help us understand why employees looking at the same event often see substantially different things" [V] (Ch 3.3, "Attributional Bias").

### Attitudes, formation, and cognitive consistency

An *attitude* is "a predisposition to respond in a favorable or unfavorable way to objects or persons in one's environment" with three components: cognitive (beliefs), affective (feelings), and intentional (behavioural intent) [V] (Ch 3.4, "Attitudes and Behavior"). The book presents two competing accounts of attitude formation: Staw's *dispositional approach* (attitudes are stable predispositions, near-personality-traits) and the *situational approach* (attitudes emerge from situational experience), with the *social-information-processing approach* of Pfeffer and Salancik as a more complicated variant (Ch 3.4, "How Are Attitudes Formed?"). Research indicates that both the dispositional and the social-information-processing views have merit, with the implication that "systematic efforts focusing on groups and interconnected social systems are likely required for successful changes in attitudes" [V] (Ch 3.4).

*Cognitive dissonance* (Festinger, presented without naming him explicitly) drives behavioural justification: when people act inconsistently with their attitudes, they experience tension and either change behaviour or change the attitude (Ch 3.4, "Behavioral Justification").

### Job satisfaction and organisational commitment

*Job satisfaction* is "a pleasurable or positive emotional state resulting from the appraisal of one's job or job experience" and is best understood in terms of discrepancy between expectations and outcomes [V] (Ch 3.5, "Job Satisfaction"). Five dimensions structure the rating literature: work itself, pay, promotional opportunities, supervision, and coworkers (Ch 3.5, "Dimensions of Job Satisfaction"). The Minnesota Satisfaction Questionnaire (MSQ) is presented as one of the most popular instruments (Ch 3.5, "Measurement of Job Satisfaction").

*Organisational commitment* is characterised by "(1) a strong belief in and acceptance of the organization's goals and values, (2) a willingness to exert considerable effort on behalf of the organization, and (3) a strong desire to maintain membership in the organization" [V] (Ch 3.5, "Job Involvement and Organizational Commitment").

## Part IV: Learning and reinforcement (Ch 4)

The chapter's opening Exploring Managerial Careers feature, "The Google Way to a Culture of Continued Learning", draws on press sources [BT, Ault; Gutierrez]. It relays the Association of Training and Development's finding that companies offering comprehensive training programmes have 218 per cent higher income per employee than companies without formalised training [BT, ATD], and holds that "Spending millions of dollars is not necessary to create a culture that promotes learning" [V]. Google's practices are presenting relevant information at the right time and in the right format, and archiving it for access at any time; sharing "dumb questions"; celebrating failure so teams learn from mistakes; and formal plans that let informal and continuous learning happen, such as pursuing one's own interests, coaching and support tools, and training on request [BT] (Ch 4, "The Google Way to a Culture of Continued Learning").

### Three models of learning

The text presents classical conditioning (Pavlov), operant conditioning (Skinner via Watson and Thorndike's law of effect), and Bandura's social learning theory as a developmental sequence [AP] (Ch 4.1). Thorndike's law of effect: "of several responses made to the same situation, those that are accompanied or closely followed by satisfaction (reinforcement) will be more likely to occur; those that are accompanied or closely followed by discomfort (punishment) will be less likely to occur" [V] (Ch 4.1, "Operant Conditioning").

Bandura's social learning theory adds *reciprocal determinism* (people control their environment as much as it controls them) and *vicarious learning* (learning by observing others' actions and consequences). Its four central elements are attention, retention, reproduction, and incentives [AP] (Ch 4.1, "Social Learning Theory").

### Strategies for behavioural change

Four reinforcement strategies are catalogued (Ch 4.2, "Strategies for Behavioral Change"):

- **Positive reinforcement**: presenting an attractive outcome following desired behaviour, contingent on the behaviour, with sufficient frequency.
- **Avoidance learning** (negative reinforcement): the desired behaviour allows the employee to avoid an unpleasant condition.
- **Extinction**: undesired behaviour declines as a result of a lack of positive reinforcement.
- **Punishment**: the administration of unpleasant consequences for undesired behaviour.

On which strategy is most effective, the text relays the answer of "Advocates of behavioral change strategies, such as Skinner": "positive reinforcement combined with extinction is the most suitable way to bring about desired behavior" [V; relayed from Skinner and other advocates, BT] (Ch 4.2, "Strategies for Behavioral Change"). The reasons given: punishment "often does not provide information to the individual about how or in which direction to change" [V] and may cause the individual to become alienated from the work situation; avoidance learning "tends to emphasize the negative" [V]. The text keeps the conclusion hedged: "A positive approach to reinforcement is believed by some to be the most effective tool management has to bring about favorable changes in organizations" [V] (Ch 4.2). Punishment can have positive work outcomes, "especially if it is administered in an impersonal way and as soon as possible after the transgression" [V], and to be effective it should "fit the crime" in severity, be given in private, and be explained (Ch 4.2, "Punishment").

The section's Ethics in Practice feature, "Detracting a Workplace Bully", draws on web and press sources [BT, University of Cambridge; Hedges; Kane]. It reports that nearly 50 per cent of employees in the US workforce face bullying at some point, and that all types of bullying, not only discrimination or harassment, matter. Angela Anderson, working for a law school administration council, was yelled at by her manager in front of coworkers, as were others; attempts to appease the manager failed, and after being threatened she was fired before she could reach HR. The feature calls the case extreme but holds that being able to take recourse against unwanted and disruptive employee behaviour is an important action for any workplace manager [BT] (Ch 4.2, "Detracting a Workplace Bully").

### Reinforcement schedules

Four partial schedules are documented (Ch 4.2, "Schedules of Reinforcement", Table 4.2):

| Schedule | Performance impact when applied | Effect when terminated | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fixed interval | Average and irregular | Quick extinction | Weekly paycheque |
| Fixed ratio | Very high and stable, reached quickly | Quick extinction | Piece-rate pay |
| Variable interval | Moderately high and stable | Slow extinction | Monthly appraisal and reward at random times each month |
| Variable ratio | Very high | Slow extinction | Sales bonus tied to selling X accounts where X varies around a mean |

The fixed-interval schedule "generally does not result in high or sustained levels of performance because employees know that marginal performance usually leads to the same level of reward as high performance" [V] (Ch 4.2, "Schedules of Reinforcement"). The text concludes that "the performance-contingent (or ratio) reward schedules generally lead to better performance than the time-contingent (or interval) schedules, regardless of whether such schedules are fixed or variable" [V] (Ch 4.2, paraphrasing Hamner). Ch 7.3 returns to the schedules and ranks them: variable ratio superior once a behaviour has been learned, fixed interval least effective (see Part VII, "Process theories").

The section closes with two further approaches to learning [BT, Kolb; Silberman]. Kolb's experiential learning style theory is a four-stage cycle: a concrete experience, observation of and reflection on it, formation of abstract concepts and generalisations, and testing them in future situations, which produces new experiences. Silberman's *Active Training* names eight qualities of an effective and active learning experience: a moderate level of content; a balance of affective, behavioural and cognitive learning; a variety of learning approaches; opportunities for group participation; encouraging participants to share their expertise; recycling concepts and skills learned earlier; advocating real-life problem solving; and allowing time for re-entry [BT, Silberman] (Ch 4.2, "Schedules of Reinforcement").

The section's Managerial Leadership feature, "Shaping a Salesperson’s Behavior", is based on a true but disguised case observed by author J. Stewart Black [AE]. Regional sales manager Sharon Johnson, with discretion over rewards from praise to gift certificates, set out to shape the behaviour of salesperson Lyle, who spent 3.5 minutes in the homes of families he judged unable to afford the books against 12.7 minutes in other homes and held back his usual sales approach with them. She planned to praise him when his times converged, expecting longer visits to bring out his typical approach, without trying to change his mind. A friend questioned whether it was ethical to use reinforcement to change people's behaviour "against their will" [V] even if they did not realise it was happening [AE] (Ch 4.2, "Shaping a Salesperson’s Behavior").

### Behaviour modification and behavioural self-management

Behaviour modification programmes follow a five-phase structure: establishing clear behavioural criteria, conducting a performance audit, setting specific behavioural goals, evaluating results, and administering feedback and rewards [AP] (Ch 4.3, "Designing a Behavior Modification Program"). *Shaping* — improving performance incrementally rather than waiting for ideal performance — is central (Ch 4.3, "Administering Feedback and Rewards").

Behavioural self-management (BSM) builds on Bandura's social learning theory, applying self-regulation through three stages — self-monitoring, self-evaluation, self-reinforcement — and four interactive factors: situational cues, the person, behaviours, and consequences [AP] (Ch 4.4, drawing on Kanfer's model). Cognitive supports include symbolic coding, rehearsal, and self-talk (Ch 4.4, "Cognitive Supports"). A field experiment among unionised state government workers reduced absenteeism through self-management training in problem identification, cause analysis, coping strategies, and self-administered reinforcement (Ch 4.4, "Reducing Absenteeism through Self-Management").

## Part V: Diversity in organisations (Ch 5)

The chapter-opening Exploring Managerial Careers feature profiles Dr. Tamara A. Johnson, assistant chancellor for equity, diversity, and inclusion at the University of Wisconsin-Eau Claire, who oversees units from Affirmative Action and the Office of Multicultural Affairs to University Police and leads campus-wide training on cultural awareness, diversity, and institutional equity [AE]. Her path ran through more than 20 years of university service, from counselling and multicultural student affairs to faculty diversity initiatives [AE]. Her goals include baseline diversity training for all faculty and staff, diversity criteria in all faculty and staff evaluations, and wider awareness of the challenges underrepresented students face [AE]. The feature closes on the chapter's point that when leaders "proactively create an inclusive and supportive climate that values diversity, benefits are produced" [V] for organisations (Ch 5, "Dr. Tamara A. Johnson").

### Three kinds of workplace diversity

The text differentiates three kinds of diversity: *surface-level diversity* "represents an individual’s visible characteristics, including, but not limited to, age, body size, visible disabilities, race, or sex"; *deep-level diversity* "includes traits that are nonobservable such as attitudes, values, and beliefs"; and *hidden diversity* "includes traits that are deep-level but may be concealed or revealed at the discretion of individuals who possess them", traits the text calls *invisible social identities* [V] (Ch 5.1, "An Introduction to Workplace Diversity").

The text projects that by 2024 white non-Hispanic participation in the labor force will decline by 3 per cent while Black participation will rise 10.1 per cent, Hispanic/Latino 28 per cent, Asian 23.2 per cent, and other groups 22.2 per cent [V] (Ch 5.2, "Race"). It catalogues specific discrimination patterns by group — discrimination against Black employees, Hispanic identity-as-whiteness dynamics, the *model minority myth* affecting Asian Americans, multiracial identity dynamics, age stereotypes, sexual-orientation discrimination, and the choice between *passing* and *revealing* for LGBTQ employees (Ch 5.2).

The section's Ethics in Practice feature, "Discrimination in the Sharing Economy—#AirbnbWhileBlack", draws on Airbnb's press room and press sources [BT, Airbnb; The Guardian; Quittner]. Airbnb presented itself as serving homeowners supplementing their incomes, but 2016 analyses found that "a significant number of hosts were using the services as though they were hotels" [V], and the feature says its structure lets it circumvent the civil rights laws that bind hotels and housing [BT]. A 2017 field experiment by Ben Edelman found guests with traditionally African American sounding names 16% less likely to have booking requests accepted [BT, Edelman]; with the #AirbnbWhileBlack campaign this led California's DFEH to file a complaint, and Airbnb reported banning discriminating hosts and eventually agreed to an audit of about 6,000 high-volume California hosts [BT] (Ch 5.2, "Discrimination in the Sharing Economy—#AirbnbWhileBlack").

The section's Managing Change feature, "Removing Bias In Recruiting", draws on press sources [BT, Grothaus; Miller]. Companies increasingly strip identifying information from applicants: anonymous applications without name or age fields, ability surveys of anonymous applicants (as at Google), or resumes with names and addresses removed and a temporary identification number assigned [BT]. Many symphony orchestras have used such blind auditions since the 1970s, in some cases with musicians behind screens; a study of 11 orchestras found that unseen auditions raised the likelihood of hiring a woman by between 25 and 46% [BT]. Other organisations rewrite job descriptions to remove terms that produce gender or other biases, sometimes with diversity experts and AI-based language analysis [BT]. Such processes can help organisations "attract more candidates, hire the best talent, increase their workplace diversity, and avoid discrimination liability" [V] (Ch 5.2, "Removing Bias In Recruiting").

### The Cox-Blake business case for diversity

Taylor Cox and Stacy Blake's framework identifies six potential competitive advantages from valuing diversity: cost advantages (reduced lawsuits, lower turnover), resource acquisition (larger labour pool), marketing (broader perspectives on consumer preferences), system flexibility (cognitive flexibility transfers to organisational adaptability), and creativity / problem-solving (multiple perspectives reduce groupthink) [BT] (Ch 5.3, "Reaping the Advantages of Diversity"). The *resource-based view* grounds the argument: diverse workforces are rare, valuable, hard to imitate, and non-substitutable, generating sustained competitive advantage [BT] (Ch 5.3).

### Theories explaining diversity outcomes

The chapter presents competing theoretical accounts (Ch 5.5, "Key Diversity Theories"):

- *Cognitive diversity hypothesis*: cultural differences yield creative problem-solving and innovation (positive view).
- *Similarity-attraction paradigm*: people prefer similar others, predicting negative diversity outcomes.
- *Social identity theory*: in-group / out-group categorisation produces in-group favouritism.
- *Schema theory*: demographic-based encoding shapes evaluation of newly encountered people.
- *Justification-suppression model*: people experience prejudice in two stages — feeling it, then either suppressing or acting on it depending on conditions (anonymity, fatigue, weak social norms).

The Watson study showed homogeneous groups outperforming heterogeneous groups overall at the first two intervals (5 and 9 weeks); by the last two (13 and 17 weeks) overall performance did not differ significantly, but heterogeneous groups generated a greater range of perspectives and more alternatives [BT] (Ch 5.5, "Cognitive Diversity Hypothesis").

### Three perspectives on workplace diversity (Ely and Thomas)

The Ely-Thomas paradigm names three orientations to managing diversity (Ch 5.6, "Three Perspectives on Workplace Diversity") [BT]:

- *Integration-and-learning perspective*: treats cultural identity as a resource for shared work and strongly links the group's diversity to the firm's success.
- *Access-and-legitimacy perspective*: instrumentalises diversity for market access; risks limiting minority members to demographic-matched roles.
- *Discrimination-and-fairness perspective*: treats diversity as moral duty without linking to productivity; can implicitly demand assimilation.

### Recommendations for managing diversity

Highly structured interviews with 15 specific characteristics (job analysis, same questions, limited prompting, longer interviews, multiple rating scales, training, etc.) reduce similarity bias when all 15 are used consistently [AP] (Ch 5.7, "Interview Selection Process"). *Diversified mentoring relationships* — relationships in which mentor and mentee differ in status — produce mutual benefits in knowledge, empathy, and skills (Ch 5.7).

The section's Managerial Leadership feature, "Diversity Training Programs", draws on research and press sources [BT, Young; Bezrukova; Anand; Lindsey]. Diversity training began with legal compliance after the Civil Rights Act of 1964, and research shows "it can be effective, ineffective, or even detrimental for employees" [V]. Training from the 1980s to the late 1990s, aimed at the needs of women and minorities, was seen by White people and men as singling them out and often backfired [BT]. Recent training on cultural competencies, valuing differences, and how diversity improves business decisions works better than focusing only on the roots of discrimination [BT]. One study found that perspective-taking and goal-setting activities kept pro-diversity attitudes and behavioural intentions in place months later [BT]. On sexual orientation, where religious rights protected by Title VII must also be respected, it advises seeking feedback from all groups and explaining the strategic and legal position [BT] (Ch 5.7, "Diversity Training Programs").

## Part VI: Perception and managerial decision-making (Ch 6)

The chapter-opening Exploring Managerial Careers feature, "Up, Up, and Away", draws on press sources [BT, Baker; Bond Street; Constine; Duff; Helm; Hyland] to follow Jen Rubio and Stephanie Korey's decisions in founding the luggage company Away in 2015. Finding no midrange option between cheap, low-quality luggage and expensive quality luggage, they researched the industry and concluded that selling directly to consumers could bring high-quality luggage to a $200-$300 price [BT]. Later decisions also rested on research: asking hundreds of people about their luggage, visiting every candidate factory before choosing a manufacturing partner in China, and pre-selling with a book of travel memoirs, on the way to $12 million in first-year sales [BT]. The feature credits their success to deciding wisely, "relying on shared knowledge, expertise, and lots of research before reaching a decision" [V] (Ch 6, "Up, Up, and Away").

### Decision-making and stakeholders

*Decision-making* is "the action or process of thinking through possible options and selecting one" [V] (Ch 6.1, "Overview of Managerial Decision-Making"). The quality of managers' decisions affects the effectiveness of the organisation and its stakeholders: "Stakeholders are all the individuals or groups that are affected by an organization (such as customers, employees, shareholders, etc.)" [V] (Ch 6.1).

The section's Sustainability and Responsible Management feature, "Brewing Sustainable Success", draws on press and research sources [BT, Crofton; Dahl; Foust; Eccles; New Belgium] to show leaders pursuing two goals at once: "doing well, and simultaneously doing good" [V]. New Belgium Brewing's cofounders cared about great beer and environmental stewardship; after an employee vote in 1999 the brewery bought all its electricity from wind power though it cost more and meant less money for employee bonuses, and it now also generates biogas from its wastewater treatment, works to reduce and recycle water, and sells used grain, hops, and yeast to ranchers as cattle feed [BT]. Citing research, the feature argues that companies committed to sustainability have superior financial performance on average, find ways to save money, and attract highly committed and engaged employees [BT] (Ch 6.1, "Brewing Sustainable Success").

### Two-system processing of decisions

The brain processes decisions through two systems: the *reflective system* (logical, analytical, deliberate, methodical, prefrontal cortex) and the *reactive system* (quick, impulsive, intuitive, basal ganglia and amygdala) [BT, citing neuropsychology research] (Ch 6.2, "How the Brain Processes Information to Make Decisions"). The text argues that "the brain can only use one system at a time for processing information" [V, citing Darlow and Sloman] (Ch 6.2). The quick, intuitive route "can be lifesaving" [V], and experienced managers can often decide very quickly "because experience or expertise has taught them what to do in a given situation" [V] (Ch 6.2, "Reactive Decision-Making"). Strong emotions pull decision-making toward the reactive route; novel and complex situations call for the reflective route.

*Emotional intelligence* — the ability to recognise, understand, and manage one's own emotions and others', which the text describes as a toggling between emotions and logic — contributes to effective decision-making (Ch 6.2, "The Role of Emotions").

### Programmed versus non-programmed decisions

*Programmed decisions* "are those that are repeated over time and for which an existing set of rules can be developed to guide the process" [V], such as ordering raw materials or setting a weekly work schedule; they support *heuristics* (mental shortcuts) that save time without guaranteeing optimal solutions [AP]. *Non-programmed decisions* "are novel, unstructured decisions that are generally based on criteria that are not well-defined", with information more likely to be ambiguous or incomplete; the text also calls them high-involvement decisions, and they "will generally need to be processed via the reflective system in our brains in order for us to reach a good decision" [V] (Ch 6.3, "Programmed and Nonprogrammed Decisions"). The six-step decision process — recognise, generate alternatives, analyse, select, implement, evaluate — applies to non-programmed decisions (Ch 6.3, "The Decision-Making Process").

### Six barriers to effective decision-making

The chapter catalogues six barriers (Ch 6.4):

1. *Bounded rationality*: cognitive limits prevent fully rational treatment of complex issues.
2. *Escalation of commitment*: decision-makers stay committed to poor decisions even as costs mount.
3. *Time constraints*: pressure pushes decision-makers toward heuristics.
4. *Uncertainty*: outcomes are unknown until alternatives are chosen.
5. *Personal biases*: the "similar to me" preference, *confirmation bias* (paying attention to information that confirms existing beliefs).
6. *Conflict*: decision-makers avoid conflict even when avoidance is harmful.

The text's conflict example is a manager who must correct a habitually late employee: the conversation will be uncomfortable, but if the behaviour is not corrected it continues, others may start copying it, and some employees may become frustrated enough to leave (Ch 6.4, "Conflict").

Conflict has two forms in this analysis: *process conflict* (about the best way to do something) "can actually lead to improved performance" [V], while *relationship conflict* "is conflict between individuals that is more personal and involves attacks on a person rather than an idea" [V]. Relationship conflict is generally harmful, in part "because feeling personally attacked will cause an individual to revert to the reactive system of the brain" [V]; managers giving feedback should keep it "focused on behaviors and activities (how things are done) rather than on the individual" [V] (Ch 6.4, "Conflict").

The section's Managerial Leadership feature, "Satya Nadella’s Transformation of Microsoft", draws on press sources [BT, Baker; Evans; McCraken; Palmer]; the text introduces it, after arguing that dealing with relationship conflict shows why emotional intelligence and empathy benefit leaders, as showing how one CEO encourages empathetic collaboration [AR]. On becoming CEO in 2014, Nadella set out to move Microsoft from a know-it-all culture to a learn-it-all one, wanting employees to "become curious and effective listeners, learners, and communicators" [V]; he asked the top management team to read Marshall Rosenberg's *Nonviolent Communication*, and tied empathy to understanding customer needs and diversity to innovation [BT]. He admitted he was wrong to suggest that women need not ask for raises [BT]. Senior team meetings moved from proving one knew all the right answers to honest opinions, regular positive feedback and continual learning, and the feature reports a more collaborative culture and improved financial performance [BT] (Ch 6.4, "Satya Nadella’s Transformation of Microsoft").

### Improving decision quality

The chapter works through the six steps for non-programmed decisions (Ch 6.5, "Techniques for Making Better Nonprogrammed Decisions"). At Step 2: "Often a manager only spends enough time on Step 2 to generate two alternatives and then quickly moves to Step 3 in order to make a quick decision" [V]; "Generating many possible options will increase the likelihood of reaching a good decision" [V] (Ch 6.5, "Step 2: Generating Multiple Alternatives"). Talking to other people and being creative help generate options. *Creativity* is "the generation of new or original ideas; it requires the use of imagination and the ability to step back from traditional ways of doing things and seeing the world" [V]; it is a skill that can be developed, and "Being creative requires letting your mind wander and combining existing knowledge from past experiences in novel ways" [V] (Ch 6.5, "Be creative").

At Step 3 the chapter recommends *evidence-based decision-making*: managers "should systematically collect the best evidence available to help them make effective decisions" [V], relying on data and information rather than intuition. The evidence may include the decision maker's own expertise and external evidence such as other stakeholders, contextual factors, and potential costs and benefits; the approach can be "particularly beneficial for new managers or for experienced managers who are starting something new" [V] (Ch 6.5, "Do you have the best-quality data and evidence?"). *Critical thinking* "is a disciplined process of evaluating the quality of information, especially data collected from other sources and arguments made by other people, to determine whether the source should be trusted or whether the argument is valid" [V] (Ch 6.5, "Are you thinking critically about the options?"). It requires recognising logical fallacies; the text catalogues seven (non sequitur, false cause, ad hominem, genetic fallacy, appeal to tradition, bandwagon approach, appeal to emotion) (Ch 6.5, Table 6.2).

Rest's four-component ethical decision-making model is presented [BT]: moral sensitivity (recognising that the issue has a moral component), moral judgment (determining which actions are right versus wrong), moral motivation/intention (deciding to do the right thing), and moral character/action (actually doing what is right) (Ch 6.5, "Are there ethical implications?"). "A failure at any point in the chain can lead to unethical actions" [V] (Ch 6.5). Moral judgment means considering whether the alternatives are right or wrong, "whether or not they will cause harm, and if so, how much and to whom" [V]; for it the text offers a front-page test: "think about how you would feel if that decision ended up on the front page of a major newspaper. If you would feel guilty or ashamed, don’t do it!" [V] (Ch 6.5, "Are there ethical implications?").

The section's Ethics in Practice feature, "Rob Ault, Project Manager, Bayside Community Church", reports the author's interview with a long-serving manager about ethical dilemmas [AE]. Ault found it hardest when what was right conflicted with his boss's instructions; he came to see that a manager is hired to benefit the company, so decisions should serve the organisation's best long-term interest as well as what is morally right [AE]. He consults trusted people: always his boss, his father (who worked in human resource management), and, in a union setting, the union steward [AE]. His father's long-term view showed that letting one person bend the rules invites others to do the same; Ault concluded "the long-term consequences of this were almost always negative" [V]. In his hardest dilemma he quit rather than do what he felt was wrong [AE] (Ch 6.5, "Rob Ault, Project Manager, Bayside Community Church").

### Group decision-making, groupthink, and devil's advocate

Group decisions reduce bias and produce more options when groups are diverse and members feel free to speak [AP] (Ch 6.6, "Advantages of Group Decisions"). *Groupthink* "occurs when group members choose not to voice their concerns or objections because they would rather keep the peace and not annoy or antagonize others" [V] (Ch 6.6, "Disadvantages of Group Decisions"). The text names two causes: "Sometimes groupthink occurs because the group has a positive team spirit and camaraderie, and individual group members don’t want that to change by introducing conflict" [V], and "It can also occur because past successes have made the team complacent" [V] (Ch 6.6). *Suppression of dissent* by powerful members produces the same effect.

Counter-measures: diverse membership, encouraging everyone to speak, assigning a *devil's advocate* to systematically critique proposed solutions, and finding common ground when conflict becomes excessive (Ch 6.6, "How to Form a Quality Group").

## Part VII: Motivation theories (Ch 7)

The chapter-opening Exploring Managerial Careers feature, "Bridget Anderson", is the case of a competent programmer at a nonprofit whose mission she believes in who, by the end of her second year, has been "motivated to do only the minimum required to get by" [V] [AE]. At her performance evaluation her manager, Kyle Jacobs, asks about her professional goals; she realises she feels isolated and became bored once past the initial learning curve [AE]. He recommends she move to an information systems team as its technical representative, and they set specific goals to satisfy her needs to achieve and to work collaboratively, including graduate classes in management and information systems [AE]. The case asks whether her motivational problems are intrinsic or extrinsic and which of her needs are unmet (Ch 7, "Bridget Anderson").

### Direction and intensity

*Motivation* is defined as "a force within or outside of the body that energizes, directs, and sustains human behavior" [V] (Ch 7.1, "Motivation: Direction and Intensity"), with two components: *direction* (what one wants to achieve) and *intensity* (effort exerted). Performance is determined by ability, motivation, role perceptions, and the performance environment; deficiencies in any one cannot be compensated by strengthening another [AR] (Ch 7.1).

### Content theories

Five content theories are presented [BT] (Ch 7.2):

- **Manifest needs theory** (Murray): humans have many needs but only a few are *manifest* at a given time; *latent* needs may exist without being expressed in current behaviour.
- **Learned needs theory** (McClelland): three needs — achievement (nAch), affiliation (nAff), power (nPow) — are learned, especially in childhood. High-nAch individuals "feel personally responsible for completing whatever tasks they are assigned," prefer "moderate" probability-of-success situations, and have "very strong desires for feedback about how well they are doing" (Ch 7.2). McClelland argues that "the high need for social power is the most important motivator for successful managers" [V] (Ch 7.2, "Need for Power").
- **Maslow's hierarchy of needs**: physiological, safety/security, social, ego/esteem, self-actualisation, with prepotency (lower needs satisfied before higher ones become motivating). The text notes that research does not support the strict hierarchical sequence [AP] (Ch 7.2, "Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs").
- **Alderfer's ERG theory**: existence, relatedness, growth, with frustration-regression (when growth needs are blocked, attention shifts back to relatedness) [BT] (Ch 7.2, "Alderfer's ERG Theory").
- **Herzberg's motivator-hygiene theory**: hygiene factors (pay, conditions, supervision) prevent dissatisfaction but do not motivate; motivators (achievement, recognition, work itself, growth) drive satisfaction. Satisfaction and dissatisfaction are on different scales [AR] (Ch 7.2, "Herzberg's Motivator-Hygiene Theory").

The section's Ethics in Practice feature, "Corporate Social Responsibility as a Motivating Force", draws on press sources [BT, Knowledge @ Wharton; Bombas; Mulvey; Barton]. CB Bhattacharya reports global employee engagement at 13 percent in 2016, against around 80 percent at Unilever, which he credits to an emphasis on a sustainable business model [BT, Knowledge @ Wharton]. His eight steps run from defining purpose and reconciling sustainability with economic goals to making sustainability visible and tying it to a higher purpose [BT]. Bombas donates a pair of socks for each pair bought [BT, Mulvey], and the Royal Bank of Scotland extended its Jump sustainability challenges to all sites after 95 percent of pilot employees said they aided engagement [BT, Barton]. The feature concludes that "adding a second, higher purpose than the established company goals motivates employees to police the company itself to be a better global citizen" [V] (Ch 7.2, "Corporate Social Responsibility as a Motivating Force").

### Self-determination theory

Self-determination theory (SDT), cited to Ryan and Deci (2000) [BT], distinguishes *intrinsic motivation* (performing an activity for its inherent satisfaction) from *extrinsic motivation* (performing for a valued outcome). SDT researchers have consistently found that "as the level of extrinsic rewards increases, the amount of intrinsic motivation decreases" [V] — has direct managerial implications (Ch 7.2, "Self-Determination Theory"). Tasks are intrinsically motivating when they satisfy at least one of three higher-order needs: competence, autonomy, and relatedness. For jobs that are uninteresting by nature, SDT would make performance contingent on extrinsic rewards; for interesting jobs, it would create more opportunities to satisfy competence, autonomy and relatedness rather than focus only on raising extrinsic rewards [AP] (Ch 7.2, "Self-Determination Theory").

### Process theories

Four process theories are presented (Ch 7.3):

- **Operant conditioning theory**: as covered in Ch 4 — reward-contingent behaviour, with positive reinforcement, negative reinforcement, avoidance learning, nonreinforcement, and punishment. Punishment "does not tell them what they should do" and "works best when reinforcement is also used" [V] (Ch 7.3, "Operant Conditioning Theory"). On schedules, behaviours learned under continuous reinforcement "are quickly extinguished" [V] once the reinforcement stops, and Ch 7.3 ranks the four partial schedules: "Which type of reinforcement schedule is best? In general, continuous reinforcement is best while employees are learning their jobs or new duties. After that, variable-ratio reinforcement schedules are superior. In most situations the fixed-interval schedule produces the least effective results, with fixed ratio and variable interval falling in between the two extremes. But remember that effective behaviors must be reinforced with some type of schedule, or they may become extinguished." [V] (Ch 7.3, "Schedules of Reinforcement").
- **Equity theory** (Adams): motivation depends on the comparison of one's outcome-input ratio against a *referent other*. Underreward inequity produces dissatisfaction and a range of restorative behaviours: alter own inputs or outcomes, alter referent's inputs or outcomes, distort perceptions, change referent, or leave the situation [BT] (Ch 7.3, "Reducing Underreward Inequity"). Two human tendencies amplify perceived inequity: people overrate their own performance, and people overrate others' outcomes (Ch 7.3, "The Basic Equity Model").
- **Goal theory** (Locke): difficult, specific, accepted goals produce better performance than easy or vague goals. *Goal commitment* is the degree of dedication to achieving a goal; participation in goal setting tends to increase commitment [BT] (Ch 7.3, "Goal Theory"). The text catalogues cautions, most of them identified by Locke: goals in one area can lead people to neglect others; unintended consequences (easy goals, unhealthy competition, sabotage); unethical use to set impossible goals; too much focus on quantified measures; and individual goals in a teamwork setting (Ch 7.3, "Goal Theory").
- **Expectancy theory** (Vroom, Lawler): motivation = E1 (effort-performance expectancy) × E2 (performance-outcome expectancy) × valence. The theory predicts that people exert the effort that yields the most positive-valence outcomes, and that motivation to exert effort is low when E1 or E2 is weak or the outcomes are not desirable enough [AP] (Ch 7.3, "The Basic Expectancy Model"). In the equation form, each outcome's valence is multiplied by its performance-outcome expectancy (E2) and summed across outcomes; combined with E1, the effort level with the greatest force is the one chosen [AP] (Ch 7.3, footnote 2). The integrative claim: "to maximize motivation, organizations must make outcomes contingent on performance" [V] (Ch 7.3, "Implications of Expectancy Theory"). *Self-efficacy* (Bandura) influences E1 strongly — "high self-efficacy employees believe that they are likely to succeed at most or all of their job duties" [V] (Ch 7.3).

The text notes that recent research demonstrates the components of expectancy theory predict performance well "without being multiplied" — refining but not overturning the model (Ch 7.4, "Expectancy Theory").

The section's Managing Change feature, "Differences in Motivation across Cultures", draws on press sources [BT, Starrfmonline; Huhman; MacLachlan]. The Ghanaian blog Starrfmonline ties motivation to employees feeling valued and supported, and describes an Eastern European case in which management coaching turned the lowest performer into a valuable team player [BT, Starrfmonline]. Consultant Pavel Vosk found that most employees go the extra mile only three times before giving up, and advises showing gratitude for effort [BT, Huhman]. Yet motivation is not one size fits all: individual recognition suits Western cultures but not Asian cultures that value the collective, and demotion motivates in Asian countries but may lose the employee in Western ones [BT]. MacLachlan warns that assuming the same incentives work everywhere "can be dangerous and have a real impact on talent retention" [V] (Ch 7.3, "Differences in Motivation across Cultures").

### Equity theory's organisational-justice extension

Recent equity research has expanded into *organisational justice*: distributive justice (fairness of outcomes) and procedural justice (fairness of the process used to allocate them). Layoffs based on seniority may be perceived as more fair than layoffs based on supervisors' opinions [AP] (Ch 7.4, "Equity Theory").

The section's Catching the Entrepreneurial Spirit feature, "Entrepreneurs and Motivation", draws on press sources [BT, Knowledge @ Wharton; Rashid; Hear from Entrepreneurs] to ask what drives people who must motivate themselves as well as others, arguing that "a lack of passion will likely kill any start-up" [V]. Yasmine El-Mehairy, who launched Supermama.me in Egypt, worked 60 hours a week on it beyond her full-time job and says that if she stops she might not get going again [BT, Knowledge @ Wharton]. Lauren Lipcon of Injury Funds Now credits purpose, giving back and a life outside work [BT, Rashid]. In a 2017 survey of 23 entrepreneurs, seven cited purpose and only one money and material success [BT, Hear from Entrepreneurs]. The feature concludes that passion and determination carry entrepreneurs through the day-to-day grind (Ch 7.4, "Entrepreneurs and Motivation").

## Part VIII: Performance appraisal and rewards (Ch 8)

The chapter opens with an Exploring Managerial Careers feature, "Two Performance Appraisal Interviews", that contrasts two reviews [AE]. Ken hands Janet a completed form rating her nearly all "satisfactory", even on dependability, though she had covered for absent colleagues three times; she leaves after 24 minutes bewildered, confused about what good performance is, and wondering whether it pays to work hard. Mary asks Ron to review his goals two weeks ahead, draws on her file of positive and negative incidents and their jointly set goals, and holds a nearly two-hour discussion in which both revise their evaluations and plan ahead; Ron leaves "more motivated than before" [V] (Ch 8, "Two Performance Appraisal Interviews").

### Uses and errors of performance appraisal

Performance appraisals serve five organisational functions: feedback, self-development, reward determination, personnel decisions (promotion, transfer, termination), and training and development needs identification [AP] (Ch 8.1, "Uses of Performance Appraisals"). Five rater errors recur: *central tendency* (lumping everyone in the middle), *strictness or leniency* (rating systematically low or high), *halo effect* (one global rating instead of trait-by-trait), *recency error* (over-weighting recent behaviour), and *personal biases* including racial, gender, similarity, and confirmatory bias [AP] (Ch 8.1, "Problems with Performance Appraisals").

### Six appraisal techniques

Six techniques are catalogued and compared (Ch 8.2):

- **Graphic rating scales**: most common (used by 57-65 per cent of organisations); susceptible to central tendency, strictness, leniency.

The section's Ethics in Practice feature, "Tesla’s Performance Review", draws on press sources [BT, Korosec; Muoio; Wattles]. Tesla's annual reviews discuss "results that were achieved, as well as how those results were achieved" [V] and feed a recognition and compensation programme with equity rewards and some promotions; in 2017 about 700 employees left after their reviews, while about 17 per cent were promoted, almost half in manufacturing [BT, Korosec; Muoio]. Elon Musk called the coverage "ridiculous" [V] and defended the standards: "if they’re not high, we will die" [V]. The box calls performance reviews of the highest importance to Tesla's success as the company keeps "pushing its employees to new limits" [V] (Ch 8.2, "Tesla’s Performance Review").
- **Critical incident technique**: supervisors record specific behaviour examples; useful qualitatively but lacks quantitative output. Table 8.2, adapted from Daft and Steers [BT, Daft and Steers], gives an example critical incident form: performance on the technology of the job (safety effectiveness; technical or specialised job knowledge) and performance on human relations (ability to communicate; results achieved through others), each with listed "possible considerations" and space for related examples, which may be positive or negative [AP] (Ch 8.2, Table 8.2).
- **Behaviourally anchored rating scales (BARS)**: behavioural anchors per scale point; reduces error sources but requires considerable design effort.
- **Behavioural observation scales (BOS)**: rating frequency of specific behaviours.
- **Management by objectives (MBO)**: jointly set goals, evaluated against actual performance.
- **Assessment centres**: multi-day standardised evaluations used for managerial potential.

The comparison table (Ch 8.2, Table 8.6) makes the cost-quality trade-off visible: rating scales are low-cost and low-acceptability; BARS, BOS, MBO and assessment centres are higher-cost and higher-acceptability. No technique is simply best: appropriateness depends partly on the appraisal's purpose, so for identifying high-potential executives assessment centres suit better than rating scales [AP] (Ch 8.2, "Comparison of Appraisal Techniques").

### Reward systems and pay-for-performance

Reward systems influence five outcomes: job effort and performance, attendance and retention, organisational commitment, job satisfaction, and occupational and organisational choice [AP] (Ch 8.4, "Functions of Reward Systems"). Lawler's four conclusions about rewards and satisfaction are reproduced:

> "(1) satisfaction with a reward is a function of both how much is received and how much the individual feels should have been received; (2) satisfaction is influenced by comparisons with what happens to others, especially one's coworkers; (3) people differ with respect to the rewards they value; and (4) some rewards are satisfying because they lead to other rewards." [V] (Ch 8.4, "Functions of Reward Systems")

Lawler's four conditions for pay to be a strong motivator: trust between managers and subordinates, accurate measurement of individual performance, substantial pay differentials between high and low performers, and few negative consequences for good performance [AP] (Ch 8.4, "Money and Motivation: A Closer Look").

The text reports that "pay secrecy may have several negative side effects" — people overestimate others' pay, lose the motivational potential of differential rewards, and lose feedback on performance — but concludes "There is no correct position concerning whether pay rates should be secret or open" [V] (Ch 8.4, "Pay Secrecy"). The Lawler study found that under pay secrecy, "almost regardless of how well the individual manager was performing, they felt they were getting less than the average raise" [V] (Ch 8.4).

### Creative pay practices

Five creative pay practices are presented with advantages and drawbacks (Ch 8.5, Table 8.7): gain-sharing (Scanlon, IMPROSHARE, Rucker, Lincoln Electric), skills-based incentives, lump-sum pay increases, participative pay decisions, and flexible benefits. The five-question test for incentive effectiveness — does it capture attention, is it understood, does it improve communication, does it pay out when it should, is the company performing better — is offered as a simple test of a plan's effectiveness [AP] (Ch 8.5, "Guidelines for Effective Incentive Programs").

## Part IX: Group and intergroup relations (Ch 9)

The chapter opens with an Exploring Managerial Careers feature, "EA Engineering, Science, and Technology, Inc.", on multiple team memberships (MTM). Citing unnamed research, the text estimates that 81 to 95 per cent of employees worldwide serve on several teams at once, which can affect focus and stress, and holds that leadership helps counter these effects [AP]. At the Baltimore-based environmental consultancy, employees work on up to six projects concurrently; working in teams gives them autonomy over their piece, leaders form naturally within groups, and employees of empowering leaders became more proactive and carried that empowerment into teams with less empowering leaders [AE]. The box concludes that at EA Engineering multiple team memberships are "a highly positive strategy to help bring the best outcome to its business" [V] (Ch 9, "EA Engineering, Science, and Technology, Inc.").

### Group definition, types, and joining motives

A group is "a collection of individuals who share a common set of norms, generally have differentiated roles among themselves, and interact with one another toward the joint pursuit of common goals" [V] (Ch 9.1, "What Is a Group?"). The 2×2 typology (formal/informal × permanent/temporary) yields four types: command groups (permanent formal), task groups (temporary formal), friendship groups (permanent informal), interest groups (temporary informal) (Ch 9.1, Table 9.1).

People join groups for six reasons: security, social needs, self-esteem, economic self-interest, mutual interest, and physical proximity [AP] (Ch 9.1, "Reasons for Joining Groups"). The text notes that office layout influences group formation: clustered offices around a central area produce more interaction than parallel rows of offices (Ch 9.1).

### Tuckman's four-stage model

Groups develop through forming, storming, norming, performing [BT, Tuckman's model] (Ch 9.1, "Stages in Group Development"). The text stresses that Tuckman does not claim all groups proceed through this sequence; the model is a generalised conceptual scheme (Ch 9.1).

### Work group structure: roles, norms, status, cohesiveness

Work roles split into task-oriented, relations-oriented, and self-oriented [AP] (Ch 9.2, "Work Roles"). A *role episode* has four stages: expected role (group expectations), sent role (communicated expectations), perceived role (individual's interpretation), enacted role (actual behaviour). The role set comprises all roles assigned to one person. Role conflict, role ambiguity, and role overload are named and deferred to later study; they return as stressors in Ch 18.2.

Group size effects on group dynamics (Ch 9.2, Table 9.2): smaller groups have higher group interaction, cohesiveness, satisfaction, and lower absenteeism, turnover, and social loafing. The relationship between group size and productivity is unclear without considering task interdependencies. *Social loafing* — individual reduction of effort on group tasks — is more prevalent in larger groups when members see their task as unimportant or simple, output as unidentifiable, or expect coworkers to loaf (Ch 9.2, "Productivity").

Work group norms have five characteristics: they summarise and simplify group influence; they apply only to behaviour, not to thoughts; they develop only for behaviours the group considers important; they develop gradually; and they may not apply to all members [AP] (Ch 9.2, "Characteristics of Work Group Norms"). Group norms serve four functions: facilitating group survival, simplifying expected behaviours, avoiding embarrassing situations, and identifying the group to others (Ch 9.2, "Functions of Work Group Norms").

The Asch conformity experiment is presented as a classic finding [BT]: "In over one-third of the trials in the experiment, the naive subject denied the evidence of his own senses and agreed with the answers given by the unknown confederates" [V] (Ch 9.2, "Conformity and Deviance"). Conformity is influenced by personality (lower in high-self-identity individuals), stimulus ambiguity, and group characteristics (pressure, identification, prior success).

Status systems serve four purposes: motivation, identification, dignification, and stabilisation [AP] (Ch 9.2, "Status Systems"). *Status incongruence* — when high status on one dimension contradicts characteristics or context — produces interpersonal hostility.

Group cohesiveness has seven determinants — homogeneity, maturity, size, frequency of interaction, clear group goals, competition or external threat, and prior success — and consequences include maintenance of membership, group power over members, participation and loyalty, and satisfaction. Cohesiveness's relationship with productivity is moderated by acceptance of organisational goals: "high performance is most likely to result when highly cohesive teams accept the goals of the organization" [V] (Ch 9.2, "Consequences of Group Cohesiveness").

The section's Managing Change feature, "Group Cohesiveness", draws on press and company sources [BT, Motivalli; Ford Media Center; Friedman]. To redesign the F-150 for 2015 with a six-cylinder EcoBoost engine and an all-aluminium body, Ford ran parallel work teams for 18 months that came together often to keep the work cohesive; the box names the teams' ability to share feedback as the most successful part and quotes Pete Reyes: "Everybody crosses boundaries" [V]. The team of over 1,000 produced a truck 700 pounds lighter with 29 per cent better fuel economy; the box credits cohesiveness with bringing Ford "to the finish line" [V] and links the close teamwork to third-quarter earnings of 1.9 billion [BT, Motivalli; Ford Media Center; Friedman] (Ch 9.2, "Group Cohesiveness").

### Intergroup behaviour: Hackman's effectiveness model

Group effectiveness is determined by group effort, group knowledge and skill, and task performance strategies — the *intermediate criteria* — themselves shaped by environmental context, design factors, and interpersonal processes [BT, Hackman's model] (Ch 9.3, "What Is Work Group Effectiveness?").

Intergroup performance depends on three interaction requirements: *interdependence* (pooled, sequential, reciprocal), *information flow* (driven by task uncertainty), and *integration* (collaboration despite different goals and time orientations) [AP] (Ch 9.4, "Determinants of Intergroup Performance"). The amount of interaction required is set by the extent and nature of the groups' interdependence. *Pooled* interdependence: groups are largely independent of one another, though each contributes to and is supported by the larger organisation. *Sequential*: the outputs of one group become the inputs of another. *Reciprocal*: two or more groups depend on one another for inputs, "thereby requiring a high degree of interaction" [V] (Ch 9.4, "Interdependence Requirements"). Five techniques manage intergroup coordination: rules and procedures, member exchange, linking roles, task forces, and decoupling (Ch 9.4, "Managing Intergroup Behavior and Performance"). Decoupling is for closely related groups that "simply don’t work together effectively" [V]: it separates them "physically or administratively" so that the organisation's required tasks are fulfilled while interaction between the groups is minimised (Ch 9.4, "Decoupling").

## Part X: Teams (Ch 10)

The chapter opens with an Exploring Managerial Careers profile, "Eva Hartmann, Trellis LLC", of one of the book's contributing authors (as the front matter lists her): nearly 20 years in HR strategy, talent and leadership development, and organisational effectiveness; founder and president of Trellis LLC, a human capital consulting and staffing firm in Richmond, Virginia; formerly global HR leader for a $600 million division of a plastic film manufacturer, leading HR managers across the Americas, Europe and Asia; and HR and quality roles at Wachovia Securities, Genworth Financial, Sun Microsystems and Andersen Consulting [AE] (Ch 10, "Eva Hartmann, Trellis LLC").

### Team versus working group

Katzenbach and Smith's definition of a team — "people organized to function cooperatively as a group" — is presented with five elements: common commitment and purpose, specific performance goals, complementary skills, commitment to how the work gets done, and mutual accountability [V] (Ch 10.1, "Teamwork in the Workplace"). A team is differentiated from a working group: the team has shared leadership, individual *and* mutual accountabilities, and measures collective work products; the working group has a focused leader, individual accountabilities, and a group purpose that mirrors the broader organisational mission.

Eight practices make teams effective: establish urgency and direction, select for skill rather than personality, attend to first impressions, set rules of behaviour, set immediate performance-oriented goals, challenge with fresh information, spend time together, and exploit positive feedback [BT, Katzenbach and Smith] (Ch 10.1).

### Team development

The Tuckman four-stage model recurs (forming, storming, norming, performing), with adjourning added in 1977 (Ch 10.2). The stages are not linear: adding a team member, or introducing a new project task that causes confusion or anxiety, can cause a slide back to an earlier stage (Ch 10.2). The Katzenbach-Smith *team performance curve* tracks the journey from working group to high-performing team.

The section's Catching the Entrepreneurial Spirit feature, "Starting the Startup Team", argues that who joins the team is among a startup's most critical questions, because human capital is its greatest asset and its resources are limited [AR]. It quotes Noam Wasserman's "Assembling the Startup Team": venture capitalists "attributed 65% of portfolio company failures to problems within the startup’s management team" [V] [BT, Wasserman]. Wasserman's "three Rs" (relationships, roles and rewards) must be managed and kept aligned: hiring trusted family and friends carries long-term hazards that outweigh the benefits, since they may think too alike; roles set decision power and status; and rewards mean splitting short- and long-term compensation [BT, Wasserman] (Ch 10.2, "Starting the Startup Team").

### Managing teams as paradox

A manager quoted in J.J. Gabarro's *The Dynamics of Taking Charge* calls building a team his highest priority yet does not write it down, since corporate would expect it anyway [BT, Gabarro]; the author reads this as typical of organisations focused on task- and outcome-driven corporate goals, when it is people dynamics and how people work together in teams that "can make a real difference" [V] (Ch 10.3, "Things to Consider When Managing Teams"). Linda Hill's framing — managing a team means managing paradox [BT] (Ch 10.3, "Things to Consider When Managing Teams"): managing both individual and collective identities and goals; fostering both support and confrontation; balancing performance and learning; balancing managerial authority with team discretion; balancing the manager-team-individual relationship triangle. A core managerial responsibility is *managing the team's boundaries* — buffering external pressure while integrating useful external forces.

The section's Managerial Leadership feature, "Who Am I Managing?", written in the first person, argues that new managers expect to manage their team but must manage every other stakeholder too [AR]. It quotes Linda A. Hill that, among new managers' challenges, "the need to reconcile different constituencies’ expectations and interests is probably the most difficult" [V] [BT, Hill; Johnson]. The author recommends a stakeholder checklist (boss, boss's boss, peers, key influencers and internal customers) to meet early and perhaps regularly, built from questions such as whose support is needed and who could keep the team from succeeding [AE].
