Such work may feel "political" but is necessary, and the answer to the title question is "EVERYONE" [V] (Ch 10.3, "Who Am I Managing?").

### Conflict, diversity, and multicultural teams

Lencioni's *Five Dysfunctions* model is presented as the framework for thinking about team trust and conflict: absence of trust sets the tone for fear of conflict, and a team that does not air its opinions through debate cannot commit to decisions — the text presents the first three dysfunctions [BT] (Ch 10.4, "Opportunities and Challenges to Team Building"). *Mining* and *real-time permission* are techniques to surface conflict productively.

Diverse teams outperform homogeneous teams on decision-making, problem-solving, and innovation according to multiple cited studies (McKinsey 2015 — top quartile for ethnic diversity 35 per cent more likely to have above-mean returns; BCG-TUM study — diversity in management correlates with innovation revenue when women exceed 20 per cent of management positions) [BT] (Ch 10.5, "Team Diversity"). A cited study found that people from diverse backgrounds "might actually alter the behavior of a group's social majority in ways that lead to improved and more accurate group thinking" [BT] (Ch 10.5).

Multicultural teams face four common conflict sources: direct versus indirect communication, accent and fluency differences, differing attitudes toward hierarchy, and conflicting decision-making norms [BT] (Ch 10.6, "Multicultural Teams"). Four interventions: adaptation (working with or around differences, when members will acknowledge them), structural intervention (reorganising to move unproductive subgroups or cliques), managerial intervention (management decides without the team; to be used sparingly, as it shows the team cannot move forward alone), and exit (voluntary or involuntary removal of a member; last resort) [AP] (Ch 10.6, "Multicultural Teams"). Cultural intelligence is "a competency and a skill that enables individuals to function effectively in cross-cultural environments" [V], developing as people grow more aware of culture's influence and more able to adapt to other cultures' norms (Ch 10.6). Lee and Liao argue that "multicultural leaders may relate better to team members from different cultures and resolve conflicts more easily" [V] and, carrying little "baggage" from any one culture, may be seen as culturally neutral [BT, Lee and Liao]. Their recommended practices are to broaden your mind, develop cross-cultural skills through practice, boost cultural metacognition, and develop cognitive complexity [BT, Lee and Liao]; the author's own global HR team opened its annual meetings with a "show and tell" gift exchange [AE] (Ch 10.6). Cultural intelligence is presented through the head-body-heart framework (cognitive, physical, emotional/motivational) (Ch 10.6).

The section's Managing Change feature, "Understanding Our Global Colleagues", written in the first person, names challenges a global team meets before cultural differences arise: time zones (calls at 8 p.m. to reach Chinese colleagues at 8 a.m.) and language, including colloquialisms "that you can’t learn in a classroom" [V] [AE]. It treats looking at situations from colleagues' cultural perspective as cultural intelligence, illustrated by Chinese colleagues finding large American meat portions unappetising [AE], and relays the HBR article "Getting Cross-Cultural Teamwork Right" on three trust-building factors: mutual learning, mutual understanding and mutual teaching [BT] (Ch 10.6, "Understanding Our Global Colleagues").

## Part XI: Communication (Ch 11)

The chapter opens with an Exploring Managerial Careers feature, "John Legere, T-Mobile", drawn from press sources [BT, Lachapelle; Roettgers; Lerman; Kovach; Chen]. Where most CEOs take reserved, scripted approaches, Legere hosts a Facebook Live podcast, appears in a magenta T-shirt and pink sneakers, and calls AT&T and Verizon "dumb and dumber" [V]. The box suggests that executives' public style likely mirrors how they relate to employees, motivating some and striking others as too much of a cheerleader [AR], and reports that call-centre employees and online forums criticised one of his press-event remarks about rivals as crossing the line. It concludes that senders "should always think through the consequences of their words" [V] (Ch 11, "John Legere, T-Mobile").

### The communication model and feedback types

The basic model — communicator encodes a message, receiver decodes it — names *encoding* (translating ideas into symbols), *decoding* (interpreting), and *noise* (factors distorting clarity) (Ch 11.1, "The Process of Managerial Communication"). Decoding "is also influenced by the receiver's previous experiences and frame of reference at the time of receiving the message" [V] (Ch 11.1, "Encoding and Decoding"), and noise "can occur at any point along the model" [V], decoding included (Ch 11.1, "Noise"). Three feedback types are catalogued: informational (non-evaluative), corrective (challenging), and reinforcing (confirming) [AP] (Ch 11.1, "Feedback").

Three types of communication are available to communicator and receiver: oral (spoken, the most prevalent), written (e-mail, texts, letters, reports, manuals and sticky-note annotations) and nonverbal (signals such as traffic lights, office size and placement, body language and facial expression) [AP] (Ch 11.2, "Types of Communications in Organizations"). Managers prefer oral communication for its efficiency and immediacy, though electronic communication is undeniably increasing, and some prefer writing for important messages such as a policy change, "where precision of language and documentation of the message are important" [V] (Ch 11.2, "Written Communication").

The section's Managerial Leadership feature, "Dealing with Information Overload", draws on press sources [BT, Gallo; Chingel; Seely]. Flatter organisations, outsourcing and integrated tools such as Slack swell the flow until "crucial messages may be drowned out by the volume in your inbox" [V], and "reply to all" multiplies the versions to read. Its suggestions: cut incoming volume (unsubscribe, turn off social-media notifications, ask colleagues to stop copying you as an FYI); file mail into folders by response timescale (inbox as holding pen, today, this week, this month or quarter, FYI) rather than by sender; and keep outgoing messages clear and narrowly copied, since colleagues follow your practice [BT, Gallo; Chingel; Seely] (Ch 11.2, "Dealing with Information Overload").

### Mintzberg's three managerial role clusters

Three role clusters from Mintzberg's seminal study [BT] (Ch 11.3, "The Roles Managers Play"):

- *Interpersonal*: figurehead, leader, liaison.
- *Informational*: monitor, disseminator, spokesperson.
- *Decisional*: entrepreneur, disturbance/crisis handler, resource allocator, negotiator. Where the entrepreneur initiates change, the disturbance or crisis handler role "depicts managers who must involuntarily react to conditions" [V] (Ch 11.3, "The Roles Managers Play").

Stewart's 1967 finding (and Guest's 1956 corroboration) that managers spend 47 per cent of their time with peers, 41 per cent within their unit, and only 12 per cent with superiors anchors the importance of liaison [BT] (Ch 11.3, "Interpersonal Roles").

### Communication as invention

The chapter advances the claim that "communication is a process of invention" — managers literally create meaning through communication. "A company, for example, is not in default until a team of auditors sits down to examine the books and review the matter. Only after extended discussion do the accountants conclude that the company is, in fact, in default. It is their discussion that creates the outcome." [V] (Ch 11.5, "Communication Is Invention"). Information never speaks for itself; context drives meaning; a messenger always accompanies a message [AR].

The Larkin and Larkin observation is reproduced: "Deep down, managers believe they are communicating effectively. In ten years of management consulting, we have never had a manager say to us that he or she was a poor communicator." [V] (Ch 11.5, "Managers' Greatest Challenge").

The section's Ethics in Practice feature, "Disney and H-1B Visas", draws on press and government sources [BT, Preston; Vargas; Boyle; Pedicini; May; USCIS]. In January 2015 Disney laid off 250 IT workers and offered a "stay bonus" of 10 per cent of salary only to those who trained their replacements over 90 days; ten-year veteran David Powers said: "When a guillotine falls down on you, in that moment you're dead" [V]. The box sets out the H-1B programme's rules and the criticism that employers displace domestic workers with cheaper foreign labour, then sets Disney's statements, framing the layoffs as a restructuring for innovation with a net gain in jobs, against the backlash, including a bipartisan senators' letter. It ends with New York Times columnist Julia Preston's verdict that "in the end it’s not about the communications, it’s about the company" [V] (Ch 11.5, "Disney and H-1B Visas").

## Part XII: Leadership (Ch 12)

The chapter opens with an Exploring Managerial Careers case, "John Arroyo: Springfield Sea Lions", a scenario with no listed sources [AE]. Arroyo, the new general manager of a minor-league baseball team, follows a much-loved predecessor, feels ostracised and powerless, and tells himself the staff will respect him in time because he is "the CEO of this ball club" [V]. After a season of falling ticket and concession sales and restless long-time staff, he wins them over by announcing that he will spend a day in each of their jobs while they watch from the general manager's box, and by creating an award in his predecessor's name [AE] (Ch 12, "John Arroyo: Springfield Sea Lions").

### Leadership versus management

Leadership is "a social (interpersonal) influence relationship between two or more persons who depend on each other to attain certain mutual goals in a group situation" [V] (Ch 12.1, "The Nature of Leadership"). Leadership and management differ on definition (leadership is a relationship; management is a process of planning, organising, directing, controlling), origin (managers appointed; leaders accepted), power source (managers from organisational position; leaders from followers' perception of expertise, attractiveness, working relationship), and motivation type (management mostly extrinsic; leadership mostly intrinsic) (Ch 12.1, "Leader versus Manager"). The text reproduces Grace Hopper's distinction: "You don’t manage people, you manage things. You lead people." [V] (Ch 12.3, "Leader Emergence").

The Ch 12.2 Catching the Entrepreneurial Spirit feature, "How a Start-Up Finds the Right Leader", draws on press sources [BT, Cohan; Casserly; Clifford; Vaynerchuk]. It argues that a start-up asks more of a leader than an established firm, since the leader must also build the relationships and processes the company needs to survive [AR]. Its case is PYP (Pretty Young Professionals), where blurred lines over Kathryn Minshew's authority as CEO ended in changed passwords and legal action; Minshew and Alex Cavoulacos, joined by Melissa McCreery, then founded The Daily Muse with a leadership plan that assigned roles by strengths and personality [BT, Cohan; Casserly]. Lawyer David Barbash is quoted: "You can have great technology but if you’re not a great communicator it may die in the lab" [V] [BT, Casserly] (Ch 12.2, "How a Start-Up Finds the Right Leader").

### Leader emergence and the five bases of power

Leaders emerge from the dynamics of need, expertise, and idiosyncrasy credits in the group [BT, Hollander, Salancik & Pfeffer] (Ch 12.3). French and Raven's five bases of power (Ch 12.3, "Leadership as an Exercise of Influence"):

- *Reward power*: people believe the holder can bestow desired outcomes.
- *Coercive power*: people believe the holder can punish.
- *Referent power*: people want to associate with or be accepted by the holder.
- *Expert power*: people believe the holder has and shares needed expertise.
- *Legitimate power*: people believe the holder has the right to influence and ought to be obeyed.

Different power types produce different responses (Exhibit 12.5): reward power elicits measured response and tit-for-tat thinking; coercive power produces alienation and resistance; referent power produces identification; rationality, expertise, and moralistic appeal produce commitment and internalisation. Research suggests rationality is the most effective influence tactic for follower commitment, motivation, performance, satisfaction, and group effectiveness [BT] (Ch 12.3). "Reward and legitimate power (that is, relying on one’s position to influence others) produce inconsistent results" [V], and "Leaders who rely solely on their legitimate power and authority seldom generate the influence necessary to help their organization and its members succeed" [V] (Ch 12.3, "Leadership as an Exercise of Influence").

### Trait approach and the great-man theory

Locke's core trait list for leaders [BT] (Ch 12.4, "Leader Trait Research"):

- Drive: high effort, achievement orientation, ambition, energy, tenacity, initiative.
- Leadership motivation: intense desire to lead.
- Honesty and integrity: commitment to truth.
- Self-confidence: assurance in self, ideas, and capability.
- Cognitive ability: conceptual skill, judgment, analytical capacity.
- Knowledge of the business: industry and technical understanding.
- Other: charisma, creativity, flexibility.

The text reports that men emerge as leaders more frequently than women, but argues "gender role is more predictive than sex" — individuals with masculine characteristics (assertive, aggressive, competitive) emerge in leadership roles, regardless of sex; androgynous individuals (combining masculine and feminine characteristics) are as likely to emerge as those with only masculine characteristics [BT] (Ch 12.4, "Sex and Gender Role"). Style differences: men are somewhat more task-oriented and more autocratic; women somewhat more interpersonally oriented and more democratic/participative.

### Behavioural approaches: Ohio State and Michigan

The Ohio State studies identified two primary behaviour dimensions [BT, Stogdill]: *consideration* (relationship-oriented behaviours: support, friendliness, openness, recognising ideas) and *initiating structure* (task-oriented behaviours: scheduling, deciding, providing direction, planning, coordinating, problem-solving, maintaining standards) (Ch 12.5, "The Ohio State University Studies"). The Michigan studies identified job-centred and organisational-member-centred behaviours, corresponding closely to initiating structure and consideration. The Blake-Mouton Leadership Grid® positions leadership styles on concern-for-results × concern-for-people dimensions; the 9,9 (high-high) style has been advocated as universally best, but the text notes there is no universally effective style [AP] (Ch 12.5, "The Leadership Grid").

### Situational approaches: Fiedler's contingency model

Fiedler's *contingency theory of leadership* assesses the leader through the *least-preferred coworker (LPC)* score (high LPC = relationship-oriented; low LPC = task-oriented) and the situation through three factors in order of importance: leader-member relations, task structure, and position power [BT] (Ch 12.6, "Fiedler's Contingency Model"). High-LPC (relationship-oriented) leaders are most effective in moderate-favourability situations; low-LPC (task-oriented) leaders are most effective in highly favourable or highly unfavourable situations.

McGregor's Theory X (people dislike work, lack self-direction, require control) versus Theory Y (people have creative capacity, can self-direct, want to participate) sets the philosophical anchor for the involvement-versus-control style continuum [BT] (Ch 12.3, "Theory X and Theory Y Leaders"). A study of 3,600 managers from 14 countries found most held Theory-X assumptions even when publicly endorsing participatory management.

### Substitutes for and neutralizers of leadership

Several factors "can substitute for or neutralize the effects of leader behavior" [V] (Ch 12.7, "Substitutes for and Neutralizers of Leadership"). Substitutes "can clarify role expectations, motivate organizational members, or satisfy members (making it unnecessary for the leader to attempt to do so)" [V], and sometimes supplement what the leader does. The text names three sources: the group member (a master craftsperson or highly skilled worker who meets their own high standards unprompted), the task (work that is intrinsically satisfying), and the organisation (work rules so clear and specific that workers know what to do without the leader) [AP] (Ch 12.7).

Table 12.1, adapted from Yukl [BT], sorts these factors by whether they substitute for or neutralise each of two leader behaviours; its column headers as printed read "Substitute Leadership" and "Instrumental Leadership" (Ch 12.7, Table 12.1). Experience, ability and training substitute in the instrumental column only; a "professional" orientation substitutes in both; indifference toward organisational rewards neutralises both. A structured, routine, unambiguous task and feedback provided by the task substitute in the instrumental column; an intrinsically satisfying task substitutes in the first column. A cohesive work group substitutes in both; low position power neutralises both; formalisation substitutes, and inflexibility neutralises, in the instrumental column; a leader located apart from subordinates with limited communication neutralises both [AP] (Ch 12.7, Table 12.1).

"Neutralizers of leadership, on the other hand, are not helpful; they prevent leaders from acting as they wish" [V] (Ch 12.7). A computer-paced assembly line stops a leader pacing the line through initiating structure; a union contract that ties pay to seniority stops merit-based pay. Neutralisers can also help: union contracts clarify disciplinary proceedings and both sides' responsibilities. Leaders should know which neutralisers are present so they can remove the troublesome ones or use their benefits, for example by developing (or convincing the organisation to develop) a better communication system when a poor one is neutralising them [AP] (Ch 12.7).

Followers also differ in *focus of attention*, defined as "an employee’s cognitive orientation while at work" [V] (Ch 12.7). It has a "trait" component (consistency in the categories of events employees think about at work) and a "state" component (minute-by-minute variation) [AP]. Research suggests that the more followers focus on off-job (nonleader) factors, the less they react to the leader's behaviours, while "a strong focus on the leader, either positive or negative, enhances the impact that the leader’s behaviors have on followers" [V] [BT] (Ch 12.7).

The section's Managerial Leadership feature, "You Are Now the Leader", draws on press sources [BT, Hakim; Yakowicz; Kauflin]. Through Toro Company senior manager Steve Keating it argues that being made a manager is an opportunity to lead rather than a guarantee of leading [BT, Hakim] (Ch 12.7, "You Are Now the Leader"), and quotes Keating: "If you don’t care for people, you can’t lead them" [V], relays consultant Carol Walker's advice to develop a job philosophy and work as a "servant leader", and reports a HighGround survey finding that managers overlook asking for feedback; asking employees "How can I be a better manager?" [V] works only if employees believe their opinion will be heard (Ch 12.7, "You Are Now the Leader").

### Transactional, transformational, visionary, and charismatic leadership

Many organisations facing chaos, culture change, empowerment and restructuring have looked for answers in "hiring the right leader" [V], and many have come to believe that the transformational, visionary, and charismatic leader is the style needed to move organisations through chaos (Ch 12.8, "Transformational, Visionary, and Charismatic Leadership").

Leaders who subscribe to "if it ain’t broke, don’t fix it" [V] are often described as *transactional*: task-oriented and instrumental, looking for incentives that induce followers into a desired course of action; they move a group to task accomplishment "by initiating structure and by offering an incentive in exchange for desired behaviors" [V] [BT] (Ch 12.8, "The Transformational and Visionary Leader"). The *transformational* leader does not cause change through inducements but inspires others "through their personal values, vision, passion, and belief in and commitment to the mission" [V]. The text names four routes: charisma (idealised influence), individualised consideration (developing the follower), intellectual stimulation (questioning assumptions and challenging the status quo), and inspirational motivation (articulating an appealing vision) [AP] (Ch 12.8).

The transformational leader is also called a visionary leader. "Visionary leaders are those who influence others through an emotional and/or intellectual attraction to the leader’s dreams of what “can be.”" [V] (Ch 12.8). Vision links a present and future state, energises and generates commitment, gives action meaning, and serves as a standard for assessing performance; evidence indicates vision is positively related to follower attitudes and performance [BT]. Citing Warren Bennis, the text holds that a vision is effective only to the extent that the leader can communicate it so that others internalise it as their own [BT] (Ch 12.8).

Transformational leaders are characterised by extroversion, agreeableness and openness to experience; they raise followers' awareness of the importance of the outcome, move them to transcend self-interest for the team, inspire self-management, and focus them on higher-order needs [BT] (Ch 12.8). In turbulent, fast-moving, competitive environments, "managers cannot rely solely on organizational structure to guide organizational activity" [V], and transformational leadership can motivate followers to internalise the organisation's goals and values [AR] (Ch 12.8). Transformational leadership is positively related to follower satisfaction, performance and acts of citizenship, because its behaviours elicit trust and perceptions of procedural justice [BT, Pillai, Schriesheim & Williams] (Ch 12.8).

*Charisma* is "a special magnetic charm and appeal that arouses loyalty and enthusiasm" [V] (Ch 12.8, "Charismatic Leadership"). The text finds it "difficult to differentiate the charismatic and the transformational leader" [V]: a transformational leader may work through the magnetism of personality, though not all transformational leaders have a personal "aura". Max Weber called charismatic leaders people with legitimate power arising from "exceptional sanctity, heroism, or exemplary character" [V] [BT, Weber] (Ch 12.8). At its extreme the leader-follower relationship involves unquestioning acceptance, affection, willing obedience, emulation and identification with the leader [BT]. The text gives the outcome both ways: Lee Iacocca's turnaround of Chrysler saved thousands of jobs; David Koresh led followers to their deaths at Waco [AP]. People working for charismatic leaders often show higher task performance and satisfaction and lower role conflict than those working for considerate or structuring leaders; charismatic leaders have a strong need for power, rely on referent power, and are extremely self-confident [BT] (Ch 12.8). The most successful couple charisma with the leadership principles other effective leaders follow; those who do not are, "at least for a time", "the pied pipers of the business world, with lots of followers but no constructive direction" [V] (Ch 12.8).

The section's Ethics in Practice feature, "Uber’s Need for an Ethical Leader", traces controversy around founder and CEO Travis Kalanick from press sources: driver protests over pay and benefits, contract drivers instead of employees, fake ride requests to competitors, sexual-harassment allegations, and a culture former employees called a "‘Hobbesian jungle’" [V]; Kalanick agreed to step down in June 2017 [BT, Lawler; Ann; D'Orazio; Fowler; Wong] (Ch 12.8, "Uber’s Need for an Ethical Leader").

### Leadership needs in the 21st century

Organisations are being re-engineered into network, virtual and modular forms, and the text expects the transition to be hard: uncertainty breeds resistance, and existing paradigms frame perception and are not easily thrown away (Ch 12.9, "Leadership Needs in the 21st Century"). It quotes Jay A. Conger: "In times of great transition, leadership becomes critically important" [V] [BT, Conger] (Ch 12.9). Conger names two forces shaping the next generation of leaders, global competitiveness in the external environment and growing diversity inside organisations, and six things effective 21st-century leaders will have to be: strategic opportunists, globally aware, capable of managing a highly decentralised organisation, sensitive to diversity, interpersonally competent, and builders of an organisational community [BT] (Ch 12.9). The text closes by calling the "mosaic" of leadership theory "far from complete", naming newer theories: leader-member exchange, implicit leadership, neocharismatic, value-based, and visionary leadership [AP] (Ch 12.9).

## Part XIII: Power and politics (Ch 13)

The chapter opens with an Exploring Managerial Careers case, "Power Play at General Electric", drawn from press sources [BT, Staley; Heath & McGregor; Sheetz; Rivas]. It traces a power struggle at the top of GE: John Flannery, appointed to revive growth after Jeff Immelt's long tenure, fired half the company's board, but after a year the board ousted him, absorbing a $23 billion loss, and named Lawrence Culp, the first outsider to lead the company [BT] (Ch 13, "Power Play at General Electric"). The text draws the chapter's point from it: although GE's circumstances may be unique, "the exercise of power and political behavior in organizations is certainly not" [V] (Ch 13, "Introduction").

### Power, authority, leadership distinguished

*Power* is "the probability that one actor within a social relationship will be in a position to carry out his own will despite resistance" [V, Weber] (Ch 13.1, "What Is Power?"). The text proposes that power is "an interpersonal relationship in which one individual (or group) has the ability to cause another individual (or group) to take an action that would not be taken otherwise" [V] (Ch 13.1).

Three types of influence are distinguished: power (ability), authority (right backed by legitimacy), leadership (eliciting voluntary response). Etzioni's typology — coercive, utilitarian, normative — classifies organisations [BT] (Ch 13.1, "Types of Power"). The French-Raven five bases recur from Ch 12, and here the text adds that referent power "has also been called charismatic power, because allegiance is based on interpersonal attraction of one individual for another" [V] (Ch 13.1, "Bases of Power").

### Power dependencies and counterpower

The extent to which influence attempts succeed depends on the target's *power dependencies*: the target's values (whether the offered outcomes matter), the nature of the relationship, and *counterpower* (the target's other sources of power that buffer the influencer) [BT] (Ch 13.1, "Power Dependencies"). The matrix at Exhibit 13.4 cross-classifies power level with dependency to predict response (compliance, bargaining, cooperation, rejection-aggression, ignoring). When B is unsure of the power relationship, ignoring A's efforts shows B either that A does have more power or that A cannot muster enough to succeed; the text's example is companies that ignored early government efforts to secure equal opportunities for minorities and women until new regulations forced compliance [AE] (Ch 13.1, "Power Dependencies").

The section's Managerial Leadership feature, "Administrative Assistants: The Power Behind the Throne", draws on press and web sources [BT, Sathian; Lawn; Price]. It presents executive and administrative assistants (EAs) as "a true example of counterpower within the organization" [V]: their bosses have power over them, but because EAs handle confidential calls, correspondence and reports, serve as sounding boards and know how the boss feels about colleagues and superiors, they hold considerable power over their bosses [AR]. Scarcity adds to it: skilled EAs have become hard to recruit and retain, Bay Area base salaries are reported to start at $80–100K, and a Pinterest EA describes a stigma attached to the title [BT] (Ch 13.1, "Administrative Assistants: The Power Behind the Throne").

### Common political tactics

Seven political tactics are catalogued (Ch 13.2, "Common Power Tactics in Organizations"):

- Controlling access to information.
- Controlling access to persons.
- Selective use of objective criteria — selecting decision criteria to shape decisions, citing Simon: "if an individual is permitted to select decision criteria, they needn't care who actually makes the decision" [V] (Ch 13.2).
- Controlling the agenda.
- Using outside experts (selectively).
- Bureaucratic gamesmanship — including *work to rule* (diligently following every rule and policy until the organisation grinds to a halt).
- Coalitions and alliances.

Guidelines for using each of the five bases of power ethically are set out in Table 13.1, adapted from Yukl [BT, Yukl]: for referent power, treat subordinates fairly and defend their interests; for expert power, maintain credibility and avoid threatening subordinates' self-esteem; for legitimate power, make appropriate requests, explain them and follow proper channels; for reward power, make feasible, ethical requests and offer only credible rewards that subordinates want; for coercive power, inform subordinates of rules and penalties, warn before punishing, punish consistently and uniformly, and punish in private [AP] (Ch 13.2, Table 13.1). The text argues that "Even coercive power can be used without jeopardizing personal integrity" [V], so managers have many tactics that need not cross into questionable behaviour; with employee lawsuits over harmful practices increasing, managers are wise to consider their behaviour before acting [AR] (Ch 13.2, "The Ethical Use of Power").

The section's Ethics in Practice feature, "Investigating the Challenger Disaster", draws on a book, an article and a newspaper report [BT, Tenbrussel & Bazerman; McDonald]. It reads the January 1986 Challenger explosion, caused by poorly designed booster-rocket seals made by Morton Thiokol, as "an example of the unethical use of organizational power" [V]. Engineers' warnings at the design stage and again in production went unheeded and the company kept the information quiet; after two engineers testified to Congress they were transferred to undesirable assignments, which both saw as retaliation, one saying, "I feel I was set aside so I would not have contact with the people from NASA" [V]. The company said it had demoted no one [BT] (Ch 13.2, "Investigating the Challenger Disaster").

### Resource dependence and strategic contingencies

The Salancik-Pfeffer *resource dependence* model: subunit power accrues to those that control critical resources others need [BT] (Ch 13.3, "Power and the Control of Critical Resources"). The Hickson et al. *strategic contingencies* model identifies three sources of subunit power: ability to cope with uncertainty (forestalling, providing information, absorbing pressure), nonsubstitutability of the unit's contribution, and centrality (workflow pervasiveness and immediacy) (Ch 13.3, "Power and the Control of Strategic Activities"). The more these three conditions hold, the more power is vested in the subunit, but the model is dynamic: citing Hickson and colleagues, the text notes that as an organisation's goals, outputs, technologies and markets change, "the patterns of power change" [V] [BT, Hickson], as subunits negotiate, bargain and compromise for a better place in the power structure [AP] (Ch 13.3, "Power and the Control of Strategic Activities"). The Lawrence and Lorsch study of three industries (containers, food processing, plastics) showed that successful firms aligned power distribution with strategic contingencies — power resided in the units most central to the firm's competitive challenges [BT] (Ch 13.3).

The section's Managerial Leadership feature, "The Politics of Innovation", draws on a book, a review and a press article [BT, Taylor; Godin; Kiechel]. It offers innovation as an example of the strategic contingencies approach: a disproportionate share of new products comes from small businesses and entrepreneurs rather than resource-rich corporations, and the text finds much of the reason in politics [AR]. New ideas inside a company meet resistance from the "not-invented-here syndrome" [V], turf fights and the urge to destroy proposals that threaten the status quo, because groups compete for money, power and promotion; as one consultant put it, "One person’s innovation is another person’s failure" [V] [BT]. The text concludes that removing politics would free energy to get innovations to market before competitors [AR] (Ch 13.3, "The Politics of Innovation").

### Politics in organisations

*Politics* is "those activities taken within organizations to acquire, develop, and use power and other resources to obtain one's preferred outcomes in a situation in which there is uncertainty or dissensus about choices" [V, Pfeffer] (Ch 13.3, "What Is Politics?"). Five conditions facilitate political behaviour: ambiguous goals, limited resources, changing technology and environment, non-programmed decisions, organisational change [AP] (Ch 13.3, "Reasons for Political Behavior"). Politics is most intense for interdepartmental coordination, promotions and transfers, and delegation of authority; least intense for personnel policies, hiring, and disciplinary procedures (Ch 13.3, "Intensity of Political Behavior").

The section's Managerial Leadership feature, "Technology, Innovation, and Politics in Performance Appraisals", draws on press sources and Adobe's website [BT, Morris; Duggan]. It holds that keeping political bias out of appraisal is hard, since managers weigh a review's effect on their relationship with the employee and on the employee's career, and "There are a lot of games played in the rating process" [V]. Its case is Adobe, which in 2012 replaced its annual review with frequent "Check-in" conversations; the text argues that ending the once-a-year cycle, and having manager and employee agree on what is formally submitted, reduces the room for politics, and reports higher engagement and satisfaction and no more negative surprises at review time [BT] (Ch 13.3, "Technology, Innovation, and Politics in Performance Appraisals").

Table 13.3, adapted from Beeman and Sharkey [BT, Beeman & Sharkey], sets out four strategies for limiting the effects of political behaviour: to reduce system uncertainty, make the bases and processes of evaluation clear, differentiate rewards between high and low performers, and tie rewards as immediately and directly to performance as possible; to reduce competition, minimise resource competition among managers and replace it with externally oriented goals; to break existing political fiefdoms, break up highly cohesive political empires by removing or splitting the most dysfunctional subgroups, and direct managers who personalise political patronage to "stop the political maneuvering" [V], removing them if it continues; to prevent future fiefdoms, make an apolitical attitude that puts organisational ends ahead of personal power one of the most important criteria for promotion [AP] (Ch 13.4, Table 13.3).

## Part XIV: Conflict and negotiation (Ch 14)

The chapter opens with an Exploring Managerial Careers case, "Conflict at Google", drawn from press sources [BT, Barr; Wakabayashi & Benner; Panchadar]. After reports that a former top executive had been paid millions on leaving Google despite misconduct and harassment allegations, CEO Sundar Pichai emailed staff that none of the 48 people fired for sexual harassment in the past two years had received severance, yet employees stayed upset. The New York Times report of a $90 million exit package for former Android chief Andy Rubin also set off external conflict between the company and Rubin, and Google updated its policy on relationship disclosure. The case calls this one step toward addressing a culture that protected executives over employees' safety and well-being [BT] (Ch 14, "Conflict at Google").

### Types and levels of conflict

Conflict is "the process by which individuals or groups react to other entities that have frustrated, or are about to frustrate, their plans, goals, beliefs, or activities" [V] (Ch 14.1, "Conflict in Organizations: Basic Considerations"). Four types: goal, cognitive, affective, behavioural. Four levels: intrapersonal, interpersonal, intergroup, interorganisational. The conflict-intensity-outcomes relationship is inverted-U: too little or too much conflict produces negative outcomes; moderate conflict can stimulate innovation, creativity, and motivation [AP] (Ch 14.1, "The Positive and Negative Sides of Conflict").

The section's Managerial Leadership feature, "Executive Conflict Resolution Strategies", draws on press sources [BT, Cringely; Harris; Flax; Byrne]. It contrasts two chief executives to show conflict as functional or dysfunctional: Jack Welch of General Electric enjoyed a good fight and, after a shouting match with a senior vice president, thanked him for standing up for his views, which Welch calls "constructive conflict" [V]; Fred Ackman of Superior Oil was accused of autocracy, treating disagreement as disloyalty and meeting it with an abusive temper [BT]. The feature adds that many now blame Welch's approach and GE's conglomerate approach for the company's fiscal problems, while others fault his successor, Jeff Immelt [BT] (Ch 14.1, "Executive Conflict Resolution Strategies").

### Causes and the Thomas process model

Seven antecedents of conflict: task interdependencies, status inconsistencies, jurisdictional ambiguities, communication problems, dependence on common resource pool, lack of common performance standards, individual differences [BT, Miles] (Ch 14.2, "Why Organizations Have So Much Conflict"). The Thomas four-stage process model: frustration, conceptualisation, behaviour, outcome [BT] (Ch 14.2, "A Model of the Conflict Process").

### Five conflict-resolution modes (Thomas)

The two-axis model — assertiveness × cooperativeness — yields five modes [BT] (Ch 14.2, Exhibit 14.4); the situations suited to each are listed in Table 14.1, adapted from Thomas (1977) (Ch 14.2, Table 14.1):

- *Competing* (high assertiveness, low cooperativeness): when quick, decisive action is vital (e.g., emergencies); on important issues where unpopular actions need implementing; on issues vital to company welfare when you know you're right; against people who take advantage of noncompetitive behaviour.
- *Collaborating* (high both): to find an integrative solution when both sets of concerns are too important to be compromised; when the objective is to learn; when merging insights from people with different perspectives; when gaining commitment by incorporating concerns into a consensus; when working through feelings that have interfered with a relationship.
- *Compromising* (medium both): when goals are important but not worth the effort or potential disruption of more assertive modes; when opponents with equal power are committed to mutually exclusive goals; for temporary settlements to complex issues; for expedient solutions under time pressure; as a backup when collaboration or competition fails.
- *Avoiding* (low both): when an issue is trivial or more important issues are pressing; when there is no chance of satisfying one's concerns; when potential disruption outweighs the benefits of resolution; to let people cool down; when gathering information supersedes immediate decision; when others can resolve the conflict more effectively; when issues seem tangential or symptomatic of other issues.
- *Accommodating* (low assertiveness, high cooperativeness): when you find you are wrong; when issues are more important to others than to yourself; when building social credits for later issues; when minimising loss when outmatched and losing; when harmony and stability are especially important; when allowing subordinates to develop by learning from mistakes.

The text reports a study in which executives typically described themselves "as using collaboration or compromise to resolve conflict, whereas these same executives typically described their opponents as using a competitive mode almost exclusively" [V]; the executives "had flattering portraits of their own willingness to satisfy both sides in a dispute" [V] (Ch 14.2, "A Model of the Conflict Process").

### Conflict-prevention and reduction strategies

Five ineffective resolution techniques: nonaction, administrative orbiting, due process nonaction, secrecy, and character assassination [AP] (Ch 14.3, "Common Strategies that Seldom Work"). Four prevention strategies: emphasise organisation-wide goals, structure tasks well, facilitate intergroup communication, avoid win-lose situations. These resemble the so-called Japanese management style, in which firms invest considerable effort in preventing conflict so that more energy is left for task accomplishment and competition in the marketplace; Intel is named as another place where much destructive conflict is prevented [AP] (Ch 14.3, "Strategies for Preventing Conflict").

The section's Managerial Leadership feature, "Sustainability and Responsible Management: Constructive Conflict that Leads to Championships", draws on press sources [BT, DeGraff; Soong; Chiari]. It holds that confrontation is "avoided only at a manager’s peril" [V], because issues that are postponed or smoothed over must eventually be solved, in sport as in business. Its case is the long feud between Los Angeles Lakers stars Shaquille O’Neal and Kobe Bryant: rather than ignore the tension or chastise the players, coach Phil Jackson built a way of playing around O’Neal's power and Bryant's speed and shooting, with a supporting cast, and the team won three NBA championships in a row [BT] (Ch 14.3, "Sustainability and Responsible Management: Constructive Conflict that Leads to Championships").

Nine reduction strategies on a behaviour-change-to-attitude-change continuum (Ch 14.3, Exhibit 14.5): physical separation, rules and regulations, limiting intergroup interaction, integrators, confrontation and negotiation, third-party consultation, rotation of members, identification of interdependent tasks and superordinate goals, intergroup training.

### Negotiation: stages, strategies, and BATNA

Four negotiation stages: non-task time, information exchange, influence and persuasion, closing [AP] (Ch 14.4, "Stages of Negotiation"). Cultural differences in stage emphasis are significant: in Mexico or South Korea, the non-task stage is longer because it establishes the relationship; in China, a signed contract may symbolise the *beginning* of final-points negotiation rather than closure.

Two bargaining strategies: *distributive* (win-lose, fixed resources, short-term) and *integrative* (win-win, variable resources, joint maximisation, long-term) [AP] (Ch 14.4, "Bargaining Strategies"; Table 14.2). Skilled negotiators differ from average negotiators in considering 5.1 versus 2.6 options per issue, spending 39 per cent versus 11 per cent of time on areas of agreement, asking 21 per cent versus 10 per cent questions, and spending 1 per cent versus 6 per cent attacking opponents [V] (Ch 14.4, Table 14.4).

Table 14.3 sets out when to negotiate seriously and when to take a take-it-or-leave-it stance: negotiate when the value of the exchange, commitment to a decision and trust are high, time is ample, the relationship between the parties is important, and power distribution is low or balanced; the opposite conditions favour take-it-or-leave-it. A footnote explains that power distribution is relative: low means one party has little power in the situation, high that one has considerable power [AP] (Ch 14.4, Table 14.3).

The *BATNA* concept ("Best Alternative To a Negotiated Agreement") from Fisher and Ury's *Getting to Yes* anchors *principled negotiation* — finding objective standards based on existing precedents [BT] (Ch 14.4, "Concluding Thoughts about Conflict and Negotiations"). "In general, the party with the more attractive BATNA gets the better of the deal. If both parties have attractive BATNAs, the best course of action may be not to reach an agreement at all" [V] (Ch 14.4).

Cross-cultural negotiation differences are documented: Americans, Arabs, and Russians differ significantly in primary negotiating style (factual / affective / axiomatic), conflict response (objective facts / subjective feelings / asserted ideals), concession-making, and deadline orientation [BT] (Ch 14.4, "Cultural Differences in International Negotiations", Table 14.5). The comparison draws on a study of persuasion styles in North America, the Middle East, and the former Soviet Union (Glenn, Witmeyer and Stevenson, "Cultural Styles of Persuasion", 1977, per the source's endnote) [BT] (Ch 14.4).

## Part XV: External and internal organisational environments and corporate culture (Ch 15)

The chapter opens with an Exploring Managerial Careers case, "Jeff Bezos of Amazon", drawn from press sources [BT, Robischon; Thomas]. It credits Bezos with what most large companies fail at, "meshing size, scale, and external opportunities with agility" [V]: Amazon was valued at an estimated $1 trillion in 2018, accounted for 44 per cent of US e-commerce in 2017, and pairs online reach with land-based distribution centres through Prime, which had over 100 million subscribers in 2018 [BT]. It also lists the challenges: shipping costs above $11 billion a year, criticism of warehouse working conditions, striking shipping contractors, possible regulation of drone delivery, and pressure to pay more taxes [BT] (Ch 15, "Jeff Bezos of Amazon").

### External environment forces

Five macro-environmental force categories: sociocultural, technological, economic, government and political, natural disasters and human-induced problems [AP] (Ch 15.1, "The Organization's External Environment"). The text catalogues current forces shaping organisations: digital technologies and AI, blockchain, sharing-economy business models (Airbnb, Uber), shifts in learning and credentialing (online courses), ethics and corporate social responsibility, climate change.

### Environment-industry-organisation fit (the 2×2)

Following Duncan and Daft, four cells based on environmental complexity (simple/complex) × environmental change (stable/unstable) [BT] (Ch 15.2, Exhibit 15.4):

- Simple-stable: soft drinks, beer, food processing, container manufacturers — low uncertainty.
- Complex-stable: universities, appliance manufacturers, chemical companies, insurance — moderate uncertainty.
- Simple-unstable: e-commerce, music, fashion clothing — high uncertainty.
- Complex-unstable: computer, aerospace, airlines, telecommunications — highest uncertainty.

### Organisational complexity

The section distinguishes external complexity, arising from the environment where the organisation operates (its country, markets, suppliers, customers and stakeholders), from internal complexity in its products, technologies, human resources, processes and structure [AP]. Leaders and managers sometimes face the dilemma of whether to grow and nurture complexity or reduce it [AP]. Drawing on De Toni and De Zan, the text gives three approaches to managing high external complexity: self-managing teams or autonomous business units with entrepreneurial responsibility to the larger organisation; simple rules that keep infrastructure and processes simple while permitting complex outputs, with Lego's five product rules as the example; and building on the company's own capabilities through open networks inside and outside the organisation, brand and reputation, and shared values, vision, strategy, processes and knowledge, developed through trust and the promotion of leaders at all levels [BT, De Toni and De Zan] (Ch 15.2, "Organizational Complexity").

### Mechanistic versus organic structures

Mechanistic structures fit stable, simple environments: top-down hierarchy of control, centralised authority, formal rules, narrow span of control, rigid departmentalisation [AP] (Ch 15.3, "Organizational Designs and Structures"). Organic structures fit unstable, complex environments: flat hierarchy, participatory communication, distributed decision-making, broader span of control, fluid task definitions.

Six organisational structures along the mechanistic-to-organic continuum (Ch 15.3, Exhibit 15.6): functional → divisional → geographic → matrix → networked team → virtual.

The matrix structure is described historically: it originated in 1960s US aerospace contracting where employees had to have dual reporting relationships with the government and the aerospace company [AP] (Ch 15.3). Matrix structures have weaknesses around divided loyalty and dual-authority confusion (Ch 15.3).

### Open systems and internal-external alignment

Katz and Kahn's open systems theory (input → through-put → output → feedback loop) frames organisations as systems exchanging resources with their environment [BT] (Ch 15.4, "The Internal Organization and External Environments"). Closed systems are insensitive to environmental changes; open systems are responsive.

The McKinsey 7-S model — strategy, structure, systems, skills, staff, style around shared values (culture) — is used as a framework for internal alignment [BT] (Ch 15.4).

### Corporate culture and the Competing Values Framework

Drucker's "culture eats strategy for breakfast" is reproduced as the framing claim [V] (Ch 15.5, "Corporate Cultures"). Culture serves two purposes: helping the organisation adapt to and integrate with its external environment by adopting appropriate values, and creating internal unity for shared goal pursuit.

The Cameron-Quinn *Competing Values Framework* (CVF) yields four cultural types on the external/internal × flexibility/control axes [BT] (Ch 15.5, Exhibit 15.21):

- *Adhocracy Culture* (external × flexibility): innovation, risk-taking, entrepreneurship — fits Facebook, Google, fast-paced industries.
- *Clan Culture* (internal × flexibility): relationships, team-building, mentoring — fits Tom's of Maine.
- *Hierarchy Culture* (internal × control): efficiency, process control, careful decision-making — fits the US Postal Service, military.
- *Market Culture* (external × control): delivering value, competing, results-driven — fits Larry Ellison's Oracle.

Amazon is presented as an instructive mixed case: an Adhocracy Culture externally (Bezos's leadership, expansion) combined with a Hierarchy Culture internally (tight control over employees at lower levels, criticised as toxic) (Ch 15.5).

### Organising for change in the 21st century

With the four external trends the 2018 Global Risks Perception Survey predicts as context (persistent inequality and unfairness, domestic and international political tensions, environmental dangers, cyber vulnerabilities), the report's authors suggest that complex organisations approach their futures with the "nine resilience lens" [V], resilience being the capacity to adapt and prosper in the face of high-impact, low-probability risks [BT, World Economic Forum]. The nine lenses fall into three categories: structural resilience, the organisation's internal systemic dynamics, which calls for "system modularity" [V] in loosely coupled structures rather than rigid, mechanistic hierarchies; integrative resilience, the organisation's interconnections with its external context, including the social cohesion it can fall back on in a crisis; and transformative resilience, where mitigating some risks requires transformation [BT, World Economic Forum]. That calls for organisational foresight, not forecasting: search, environmental scanning and discovery techniques, innovation and experimentation, "to engage with the uncertainty of multiple futures" [V] (Ch 15.6, "Organizing for Change in the 21st Century").

## Part XVI: Organisational structure and change (Ch 16)

The chapter opens with an Exploring Managerial Careers profile of Jackie Smith, vice president of CareSource University at CareSource, a Medicaid managed care organisation, where she also oversees the company’s performance management, succession and goal-setting processes [AE] (Ch 16, "Jackie Smith, CareSource University"). The profile reports that in 2017 the university delivered more than 240,000 learning hours, coached 300 leaders and onboarded 1,100 new hires, and lists the leadership-development programmes she designed, among them "Leading through Extraordinary Change" [V] and "Building Sustainable Strategy with Appreciative Inquiry" [V]. Before CareSource she ran a performance-consulting firm and held organisational development, HR and training roles in financial services, retail and transportation [AE] (Ch 16, "Jackie Smith, CareSource University").

### Bureaucracy and the mechanistic-organic continuum

Weber's five bureaucratic elements — specialisation, command-and-control, span of control, centralisation, formalisation — are presented as the foundation for organisational design [BT] (Ch 16.1, "Bureaucracy"). The mechanistic / organic distinction is reframed (Ch 16.1, Table 16.1): high standardisation, narrow specialisation, centralised, functional departmentalisation = mechanistic; the opposites = organic.

### Three types of change and the organisational life cycle

Three types of organisational change: structural (formal relationships), technological (new technologies), and culture (most difficult, requires reshaping core identity) [AP] (Ch 16.2, "Types of Change").

The four-phase organisational life cycle: entrepreneurship (loose, organic) → survival and early success (structures emerge) → sustained success / maturity (mechanistic structures strengthen, functional structures introduced) → renewal or decline (further-flung operations, autonomy, possible restructuring) [AP] (Ch 16.2, "The Organizational Life Cycle"). The implication: structural needs evolve over time; the ideal structure changes.

### Three dimensions of change

Three dimensions for assessing change (Ch 16.2, "Dimensions of Change"):

- *Scope*: incremental (small refinements, LEAN, Six Sigma) versus transformational (significant, disruptive).
- *Level*: individual / group / organisation.
- *Intentionality*: planned versus unplanned (emergent).

### Four common change models

Four change models with different assumptions [BT] (Ch 16.3):

- **Lewin's three-stage model**: unfreeze → change → refreeze. Most understandable when the organisation is assumed to be generally stable, a context the text calls increasingly rare.
- **Kotter's eight-step model**: establish urgency → form guiding coalition → create vision → communicate vision → remove obstacles → create small wins → consolidate improvements → anchor changes. Mechanistic, top-down, deficit-based assumptions; high-control situations.
- **Cooperrider's Appreciative Inquiry (AI)**: 5-D cycle (define, discover, dream, design, destiny). Abundance-based, bottom-up, positive. Uses appreciative conversations to shift organisational narratives: people "work together to co-create a positive vision of an ideal future for their organization" [V], and employees envision the changes they want to see, "then work together to design how they will make these changes a reality" [V] (Ch 16.3, "Common Change Models").
- **Olson and Eoyang Complex Adaptive Systems (CAS)**: organisations are emergent, self-organising. Three influence levers: empower change agents, strengthen connections among people, ensure information and energy flow through connections. Self-organising structures can be altered through boundary conditions, disturbances, and connection-and-flow attention.

The text argues that the perception of the organisation's state (deficit-based versus abundance-based), the mechanism of change (top-down versus bottom-up), and the mindset toward people (conventional versus appreciative) jointly shape which model fits (Ch 16.3, "Basic Assumptions about Change").

The section's Sustainability and Responsible Management feature, "Why Is the National Hockey League Interested in Climate Change, and Why Did They Hire Kim Davis?", draws on press sources [BT, Larkin; Blackistone; Green; Benjamin]. It presents the NHL's appointment of Kim Davis, a Black woman from outside hockey culture, as executive vice president of social impact, growth initiatives and legislative affairs as a shift towards inclusivity in a league run mostly by White men [BT]. Davis, who prepared employees for nine mergers at JPMorgan Chase, says people "aren’t comfortable with change happening to them" [V]. The feature also relays Gary Bettman's account of NHL Green, prompted by a game that needs cold weather and fresh water, and former player Andrew Ference's sustainability initiatives [BT] (Ch 16.3, "Why Is the National Hockey League Interested in Climate Change, and Why Did They Hire Kim Davis?").

## Part XVII: Human resource management (Ch 17)

The chapter opens with an Exploring Managerial Careers profile of Eva Hartmann, founder and president of Trellis LLC, a human capital consulting and staffing firm in Richmond, Virginia [AE] (Ch 17, "Eva Hartmann, Trellis LLC"). She began her career at a Big 6 management consulting firm and, before Trellis, was global HR leader for a plastic film manufacturer's $600 million division, leading HR managers across North and South America, Europe and Asia; she has also held HR and quality roles at Wachovia Securities, Genworth Financial, Sun Microsystems and Andersen Consulting [AE]. The profile calls her "a transformational change agent" [V] with expertise in HR strategy, talent and leadership development, and organisational effectiveness (Ch 17, "Eva Hartmann, Trellis LLC").

### Four waves of HR

Ulrich, Younger, Brockbank, and Younger's four-wave evolution of HR work [BT] (Ch 17.1, "An Introduction to Human Resource Management"):

- Wave 1: administrative work (terms and conditions, regulatory compliance).
- Wave 2: design of innovative HR practices (compensation, learning, communication, sourcing).
- Wave 3: integration of HR strategy with business strategy.
- Wave 4: HR as a competitive practice responding to external customer, investor, and community demands.

The section's Catching the Entrepreneurial Spirit feature, "Human Resources Outsourcing—Entrepreneurial Ventures", argues that small companies whose staff lack the bandwidth or expertise for employee relations, benefits and payroll, or HR compliance increasingly outsource HR, drawing HR practitioners into entrepreneurial ventures [AR]. Beyond long-outsourced benefits and payroll, "fractional HR" [V] supplies HR services on a part-time or intermittent basis, from compliance and training to talent-management processes such as performance management and succession planning [AP]. Two factors drive the decision, "time and risk" [V]: a leader spending too much time on HR issues, and exposure to lawsuits [AP]. The feature calls fractional HR and HR outsourcing a viable and financially rewarding business model for HR entrepreneurs [AR] (Ch 17.1, "Human Resources Outsourcing—Entrepreneurial Ventures").

For compliance, Ch 17.2 gives a partial list of federal labour laws by number of employees, as displayed on the SHRM website, naming eleven laws that cover all employees of all organisations: the American Taxpayer Relief Act (2012), Consumer Credit Protection Act (1968), Employee Polygraph Protection Act (1988), Employee Retirement Income Security Act (1974), Equal Pay Act (1963), Fair and Accurate Credit Transaction Act (2003), Fair Credit Reporting Act (1969), Fair Labor Standards Act (1938), Federal Insurance Contributions Act (1935), Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (1996, where a company offers benefits) and Immigration Reform and Control Act (1986). Whether the employer is public or private, offers health insurance, or uses a third party for background checks may also bear on coverage [BT, SHRM] (Ch 17.2, Table 17.1).

### Performance management evolution and current debates

The performance management process traces back to the US military's WWI "merit rating" system; from 1981 Jack Welch championed forced ranking at GE, "another military creation" ("A" players rewarded, "C" players dismissed) [BT] (Ch 17.3, "Performance Management"). The text reports widespread dissatisfaction: 58 per cent of executives surveyed by Deloitte believed their performance management approach drove neither engagement nor high performance.

Deloitte's "radical redesign" replaced traditional ratings with four forward-looking questions about each individual: highest possible compensation increase, always want this person on the team, at risk for low performance, ready for promotion today (Ch 17.3, "Performance Management").

The section's Managing Change feature, "Global versus Local HR", argues that multinationals are well served by keeping global standards while allowing local adaptation in the HR areas where it makes most sense [AR]. Citing a 2012 MIT Sloan Management Review article [BT], it reports that most multinationals set performance standards, competency profiles and performance management tools globally, as the areas most closely linked to strategy, while training and compensation may need local input and hiring may need local adaptation for country-specific labour laws [BT]. Too many country-specific adaptations for top talent limit global talent management; global leadership and rotational programmes let a company "pollinate the business with talented employees from around the globe" [V] (Ch 17.3, "Global versus Local HR").

### Pay-for-performance and total rewards

A 2011 SHRM article by Stephen Miller reports four drivers for moving to pay-for-performance: recognise and reward high performers (46.9%), increase likelihood of achieving corporate goals (32.5%), improve productivity (7.8%), move away from entitlement culture (7.8%) [AP] (Ch 17.4).

WorldatWork's six total-rewards elements: compensation, benefits, work-life effectiveness, recognition, performance management, talent development [AP] (Ch 17.4, "Influencing Employee Performance and Motivation"). The Nohria-Groysberg-Lee four-drives model maps drives (acquire, bond, comprehend, defend) to organisational levers (reward systems, culture, job design, performance management and resource allocation) [BT] (Ch 17.4).

### Talent acquisition and succession planning

The Fernandez-Araoz / Groysberg / Nohria six-step recruiting framework — anticipate, specify the job, develop the pool, assess candidates, close the deal, integrate the newcomer [BT] (Ch 17.5).

The 9-box talent review template (performance × potential) anchors talent reviews, with potential defined as "an employee's ability to demonstrate the behaviors necessary to be successful at the next highest level within the company" [V] (Ch 17.6, "Talent Development and Succession Planning"). Succession planning identifies short-term (<1 year), mid-term (1-3 years), and long-term (3+ years) successor candidates per role. Follow-up development tools: training, stretch assignments, individual assessments (including 360-degree feedback), individual development plans.

The section's Managing Change feature, "Tech in Human Resources", argues that HR professionals need to track a boom in HR technology driven by mobile technology, social media, data analytics and learning management [AR]. Drawing on Josh Bersin's SHRM.org article "9 HR Tech Trends for 2017" [BT, Bersin], it describes performance management tools that replace the once-a-year process with ongoing, real-time tracking, team-based management, pulse surveys and goal tracking; the "rise of people analytics" [V], including predictive tools for job-change outcomes and security leaks and a badge that detects employee stress from voice; and a shift from learning management to scaled, video-based online learning [BT, Bersin]. The author calls investment in human capital one of the most critical a company makes [AR] (Ch 17.6, "Tech in Human Resources").

## Part XVIII: Stress and well-being (Ch 18)

The chapter opens with an Exploring Managerial Careers feature, "Workplace Perks: Are They Worth It?", drawn from press and survey sources [BT, Rao; Ivanova; Covert]. It reports PayScale research that big tech companies such as Facebook and Amazon can expect more turnover from low job satisfaction and job meaning, with Amazon's reported stress above the tech average, 64 per cent against 58 per cent [BT]. It ties the stress to long hours, weekend work and staying connected to e-mail 24/7, quoting Gartner analyst Lydia Leong: "Amazon is a culture of self-driven workaholics" [V]. It cites American Institute of Stress symptom figures and a World Health Organization estimate that stress costs businesses $300 billion a year [BT], and concludes that managers must commit energy and resources to minimise the dysfunctional consequences of stress [AR] (Ch 18, "Workplace Perks: Are They Worth It?").

### Stress definition, general adaptation syndrome, and intensity-J-curve

Stress is "a physical and emotional reaction to potentially threatening aspects of the environment" — a poor person-environment fit [V] (Ch 18.1, "Work-Related Stress"). The damage from stress is *strain*. Selye's general adaptation syndrome: alarm → resistance → exhaustion [BT] (Ch 18.1, "General Adaptation Syndrome").

Stress and performance follow an inverted-J: low or moderate stress can stimulate motivation and performance; very high stress consumes attention and energy, dropping performance markedly [AP] (Ch 18.3, "Stress and Job Performance"). Some stress is necessary for psychological growth, creative activity, and skill acquisition.

### Two stress types

*Frustration* is "a psychological reaction to an obstruction or impediment to goal-oriented behavior" — what happens when a person wants to do something but is prevented [V] (Ch 18.1, "Types of Stress: Frustration and Anxiety"). *Anxiety* is "a feeling of inability to deal with anticipated harm" — what happens when one lacks plans or coping responses for anticipated problems.

### Organisational influences on stress

Four major organisational stressors (Ch 18.2):

- Occupational differences: high-stress occupations are typified by little control, relentless time pressures, threatening physical conditions, or major responsibility for human or financial resources. Top of high-stress list: firefighter, race car driver, astronaut, surgeon, NFL football player. Low-stress: musical instrument repairperson, medical records technician, librarian (Ch 18.2, Table 18.1).
- Role ambiguity: inadequate information about one's role; documented in 35-60 per cent of employees in two surveys; produces psychological strain, dissatisfaction, underutilisation, futility.
- Role conflict: simultaneous incompatible expectations.
- Role overload (quantitative or qualitative) and role underutilisation: visualised as a continuum where the optimum is a person-environment fit (Ch 18.2, Exhibit 18.4).

### Personal influences and Type A personality

Three personal stress factors (Ch 18.2, "Personal Influences on Stress"):

- *Personal control*: extent to which the employee has control over factors affecting performance. Internal locus of control intensifies the negative response to constrained control; externals are less affected.
- *Type A personality* (Friedman and Rosenman): impatience, restlessness, aggressiveness, competitiveness, polyphasic activities, time pressure. The Rosenman-Friedman 8.5-year study of 3,500 men found Type A individuals "twice as prone to heart disease, five times as prone to a second heart attack, and twice as prone to fatal heart attacks" compared to Type B [V] (Ch 18.2, "Type A Personality"). Approximately 60 per cent of managers in one study were Type A; only 12 per cent clearly Type B. The text notes the irony: Type A behaviour is helpful for promotion to the top but can be detrimental once there.
- *Rate of life change* (Holmes and Rahe): higher rates of life change are correlated with stress and illness onset.

### Buffering effects: social support and hardiness

*Social support* — peer trust and concern — buffers stress effects [BT, citing medical research] (Ch 18.3, "Social Support"). Medical studies consistently found that high peer support reduced negative outcomes of potentially stressful events and increased positive outcomes [BT], from which the text infers that managers should value "building cohesive, supportive work groups—particularly among individuals who are most subject to stress" [V] (Ch 18.3, "Social Support"). *Hardiness* — a collection of personality characteristics including commitment, internal locus of control, and a sense of life challenge — moderates stress; "people characterized by hardiness have a clear sense of where they are going and are not easily deterred by hurdles" [V] (Ch 18.3, "Hardiness").

The section's Managerial Leadership feature, "Disconnecting from the “Always On” Work Culture", draws on press sources [BT, Caldwell; O'Connor; Kitchen; Wall]. It links constant smartphone reachability for work to high stress and negative health effects [BT], citing an Academy of Management study in which employees "tally an average of 8 hours a week answering work-related emails after leaving the office" [V] and UK surveys in which 72.4 per cent of respondents performed work tasks outside regular hours [BT]. Device use in the two hours before bed, and blue light, can disrupt sleep [BT]. France's "right to disconnect" [V] law, in force from 1 January 2017, bars employers from firing employees who do not respond to work inquiries while out of office [BT] (Ch 18.3, "Disconnecting from the “Always On” Work Culture").

### Consequences of stress

High stress contributes to: heart disease, peptic ulcers, arthritis, mental illness; counterproductive behaviours including turnover, absenteeism, alcoholism, drug abuse, aggression, and sabotage; performance decline; and burnout [AP] (Ch 18.3, "Consequenses of Work Related Stress"). *Burnout* is "a general feeling of exhaustion that can develop when a person simultaneously experiences too much pressure to perform and too few sources of satisfaction" [V] (Ch 18.3, "Stress and Burnout").

## Part XIX: Entrepreneurship (Ch 19)

The chapter opens with an Exploring Managerial Careers feature on Maria Rose Belding, drawn from press sources [BT, Belding; Du; Dunham; Fournier; McCoy]. Made to throw out hundreds of boxes of expired macaroni and cheese while volunteering at a food shelter as a middle school student, Belding created MEANS (Matching Excess and Need for Stability) Database, a nonprofit online network that matches food pantries and shelters with donors of surplus food such as restaurants, grocery stores and caterers [BT]. Cofounder Grant Nelson built its cloud infrastructure, and pantries can post unsuitable donations for another pantry to claim [BT]. MEANS has moved over two million pounds of food across 48 states [BT]. The chapter then introduces Belding as one of millions of the world's entrepreneurs [AE] (Ch 19, "Maria Rose Belding, MEANS Database").

### Six types of entrepreneurship

Entrepreneurs are "individuals who recognize and pursue opportunities, take on risk, and convert these opportunities into value-added ventures that can survive in a competitive marketplace" [V] (Ch 19, Introduction). Six types are catalogued (Ch 19.1):

- *Social entrepreneurship*: innovative solutions to social or environmental problems.
- *Corporate entrepreneurship*: new products, processes, ventures within large organisations.
- *Family entrepreneurship*: business owned and managed by multiple family members across generations.
- *Serial or habitual entrepreneurship*: starting multiple businesses.
- *Lifestyle entrepreneurship*: ventures suiting a personal lifestyle.
- *High-technology entrepreneurship*: ICT ventures, typically high growth expectations.

### GEM stages and the Total Entrepreneurial Activity (TEA) rate

The Global Entrepreneurship Monitor identifies four entrepreneurial stages: potential (capacity and intention), nascent (<3 months), new business owner (3 months to 3 years), established business owner (3.5+ years) [AP] (Ch 19.1, "Global Entrepreneurship Prevalence"). TEA varies from <5 per cent in Bulgaria, Bosnia & Herzegovina, Italy, Japan to ~20 per cent in Ecuador.

### Entrepreneurial personality traits

Nine entrepreneurial traits: ambitious, independent, self-confident, risk-taking, visionary, creative, energetic, passionate, committed [AP] (Ch 19.2, "Entrepreneurial Personality"). The text notes that entrepreneurs also need technical knowledge and managerial ability (Ch 19.2, "Managerial Ability and Technical Knowledge").

The section's Ethics in Practice feature, "Ethical Choices Transform Family Business into International Brand", draws on press sources [BT, Bortin; Collins; Katz; Antoine]. Apollonia Poilâne took over her family's Paris bakery at 18, after her parents died in a 2002 helicopter crash, and ran it from Cambridge, Massachusetts, while studying at Harvard; her admissions essay said "The work of several generations is at stake." [V]. Her father Lionel had built the business her grandfather established in 1932 into a global brand, with sourdough as its signature product [BT]. Describing herself as the "commander of the ship" [V], she kept control of strategy; Poilâne is reported as an $18 million business with 160 employees, shipping more than 200,000 loaves a year to clients in 20 countries [BT] (Ch 19.2, "Ethical Choices Transform Family Business into International Brand").

### The business model canvas

Osterwalder's business model canvas covers four areas — customers, offering, infrastructure, financial viability — through nine building blocks [BT] (Ch 19.3, "Business Model Canvas"):

- Customer segments.
- Value propositions.
- Channels.
- Customer relationships.
- Revenue streams.
- Key resources.
- Key activities.
- Key partnerships.
- Cost structure.

The Apple example illustrates: mass-market customer segment, seamless music experience as value proposition, retail/online channels, lovemark customer relationship, hardware revenue stream, brand-and-content key resources, marketing and design key activities, OEM partnerships, manufacturing-and-marketing cost structure (Ch 19.3, Table 19.2).

### First mover versus second mover and design thinking

First movers can define category characteristics, capture name recognition, lock in distribution channels, set technology standards. Second movers learn from and improve on first-mover efforts. "Research on the battle between first and second movers indicates that they are equally likely to win the market" [V] (Ch 19.3).

The Ch 19.4 Catching the Entrepreneurial Spirit feature, "Making a Heavenly Deal", gathers press advice on attracting angel investors [BT, Kawasaki; Newlands; Emerson; Fallon; Zhao; Abrams]: show them a business from an industry they understand; know the figures (annual sales, gross profit, profit margin, expenses); describe the business in under a minute and limit presentations to 10 slides; mind timing and the angel's sector interests; present a competent management team with a strong, experienced leader; offer room for the angel to add value, for example through a board seat; and emphasise likely exits, the competition, and how the cash will win market share [BT] (Ch 19.4, "Making a Heavenly Deal").

*Design thinking* uses elements of play, empathy, reflection, creation, and experimentation across three phases: inspiration (the design challenge), ideation (creative solving), implementation (turning ideas into actions) [AP] (Ch 19.5). Convergent thinking narrows from broad to specific; divergent thinking opens new possibilities.

### Government support for entrepreneurship

Government can support entrepreneurship through reducing regulatory barriers, protecting intellectual property and capital, providing commercialisable technology, increasing positive incentives (subsidies, training programmes), or providing special benefits to favoured industries (cronyism — comes at a political and economic cost) [AP] (Ch 19.6).

The section's Managing Change feature, "Technology and Innovation: The Right Stuff", based on a case by Siri Terjesen [BT, Terjesen], illustrates government making federal-lab technology available for commercialisation. After a corporate career of more than 25 years, David Belaga licensed NASA scientist John Greenleaf's patented formula for rehydrating astronauts, which research suggested would also suit athletes facing dehydration, through NASA's Technology Partnership Division, which prioritises small business partnerships [BT]. After a 150-page business plan and a 60-day public comment period, he won exclusive rights, with royalties for NASA and a guarantee of U.S. production [BT]. Funded with $300,000 of his own money and $325,000 from friends and family, he focused on institutional buyers; the product is now used by most professional North American sports teams and hundreds of U.S. universities [BT] (Ch 19.6, "Technology and Innovation: The Right Stuff").

## Appendix A: Scientific method in OB research

Five research designs in increasing rigor and cost [AP] (Appendix A, "Basic Research Designs"):

- Naturalistic observation (authoritative opinions, case studies): low rigor, low cost, no a priori hypotheses, qualitative.
- Survey research: low control, high external validity, low cost, qualitative and quantitative.
- Field study: medium control, high external validity, medium cost, quantitative.
- Field experiment: high control, high external validity, high cost, quantitative.
- Laboratory experiment: high control, low external validity, high cost, quantitative.

Five criteria for evaluating a theory (Kaplan): internal consistency, external consistency, scientific parsimony, generalisability, verification [BT] (Appendix A, "What Is a Good Theory?"). The text quotes Lewin: "There is nothing so practical as a good theory" [V] (Appendix A, "Uses of a Theory").
