## Connections the authors make in the text

- *Bounded rationality*: presented as foundational for understanding decision limits, with no originator named (Ch 6.4, "Bounded Rationality"). Herbert Simon is cited on the selective use of decision criteria [BT] (Ch 13.2) and, with Dearborn, for the selective-perception study [BT] (Ch 3.1).
- *Maslow's hierarchy of needs* and *McGregor's Theory X/Y*: positioned as foundational, with the text noting research does not strictly support Maslow's hierarchical sequencing [BT] (Ch 7.2; Ch 12.3).
- *Hofstede's cultural programming* and *Kluckhohn-Strodtbeck's six cultural dimensions*: core comparative-management framing [BT] (Ch 2.7).
- *Argyris's basic incongruity thesis*: anchors the personality-organisation conflict treatment [BT] (Ch 2.5).
- *Tuckman's stages*: cited in two chapters (Ch 9 and Ch 10) for group/team development [BT].
- *Mintzberg's managerial roles*: anchors the communication chapter [BT] (Ch 11.3).
- *French and Raven's bases of power*: cited in two chapters (Ch 12.3, Ch 13.1) [BT].
- *Vroom expectancy theory* and *Adams equity theory*: foundational for motivation and rewards [BT] (Ch 7.3, Ch 8).
- *Festinger's cognitive dissonance*: mentioned without explicit naming [BT] (Ch 3.4).
- *Pavlov, Skinner, Thorndike, Bandura*: learning theory lineage [BT] (Ch 4).
- *Fiedler's contingency theory* and *House and Evans's path-goal theory*: the two situational theories Ch 12.6 explores; Hersey and Blanchard's life cycle theory is named only in a list of situational theories [BT] (Ch 12.6).
- *Lewin's change model* and *Kotter's eight-step model*: planned change processes, one of the first and one of the most widely used [BT] (Ch 16.3).
- *Cooperrider's Appreciative Inquiry*: bottom-up emergent change [BT] (Ch 16.3).
- *Cox and Blake's business case for diversity*: anchors Ch 5.3 [BT].
- *Ely and Thomas's three perspectives on diversity*: anchors Ch 5.6 [BT].
- *Salancik and Pfeffer's resource dependence model*: power distribution analysis [BT] (Ch 12.3, Ch 13.3).
- *Hickson et al. strategic contingencies model*: subunit power [BT] (Ch 13.3).
- *Lawrence and Lorsch contingencies study*: industry-power alignment [BT] (Ch 13.3).
- *Cameron and Quinn's Competing Values Framework*: cultural typology [BT] (Ch 15.5).
- *Katz and Kahn's open systems theory*: organisation-environment exchange [BT] (Ch 15.4).
- *Friedman and Rosenman's Type A research*: stress and heart disease [BT] (Ch 18.2).
- *Holmes and Rahe's life-change scale*: stress-illness link [BT] (Ch 18.2).
- *Kanter's symbols of managerial power*: power markers [BT] (Ch 13.2).
- *Fisher and Ury's Getting to Yes / BATNA / principled negotiation*: cited approvingly [BT] (Ch 14.4).
- *Osterwalder's business model canvas*: framework adopted for entrepreneurship [BT] (Ch 19.3).
- *Katzenbach and Smith on team discipline*: foundational for team chapter [BT] (Ch 10).
- *Lencioni's Five Dysfunctions*: team-trust framework [BT] (Ch 10.4).
- *Drucker on language and culture*: quoted in two chapters [BT] (Ch 11.4, Ch 15.5).

## Positions the authors explicitly frame against

- *Punishment as primary reinforcer*: the text cautions that punishment's use "must be carefully considered and implemented" [V] and relays the view of Skinner and other advocates that positive reinforcement combined with extinction is the most suitable approach [BT] (Ch 4.2).
- *Strict Maslow hierarchical sequencing*: research does not support the strict prepotency claim [AR] (Ch 7.2, "Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs").
- *Treating employees identically (equality) regardless of performance*: in its treatment of expectancy theory the text argues that organisations subscribing too strongly to equality ("not to be confused with equity") leave employees with weak performance-outcome expectancies (E2s), because no distinctions are made for differential outcomes [AR] (Ch 7.3, "Expectancy Theory").
- *Conflict as inherently destructive*: the text argues that moderate conflict can be productive and that process conflict (about how to do something) can improve performance, in contrast to relationship conflict [AR] (Ch 6.4, Ch 14.1).
- *Stereotyping in employment decisions*: stereotypes are defined as overgeneralisations about large groups, and "Stereotypes are the basis for prejudice and discrimination" [V]; using them in employment decision-making is often illegal and, illegal or not, inconsistent with valuing diversity [AR] (Ch 5.5). Similarity and other personal biases are listed among appraisal errors (Ch 8.1).
- *Forced ranking as a long-term performance management tool*: the text notes GE backed away from it after Welch retired and many companies followed because it "fostered internal competition and undermined collaboration and teamwork" [V] (Ch 17.3).
- *Top-down change as universally appropriate*: the text contrasts conventional top-down change with bottom-up appreciative and complex-adaptive approaches, arguing that "the more complex the potential change, the greater the need to involve employees" [V] (Ch 16.3).
- *Strategy as more influential than culture*: the text quotes Drucker's "culture eats strategy for breakfast" [V] and glosses it as meaning that corporate culture is more influential than strategy in motivating employees' beliefs, behaviours, relationships and ways of working [AR] (Ch 15.5).

## Citation and source-integrity notes

This deep reference was produced under the 9-pass ingestion protocol from the converted markdown of the OpenStax PDF as converted with pymupdf4llm 0.2.9 from the OpenStax PDF (631 pages), with the Ch 12 spans restored by hand. The source has since been re-converted in full (2026-10-16, PyMuPDF text blocks; see the source card).

**Conversion path.** This reference was read from a pymupdf4llm 0.2.9 conversion (markitdown 0.1.5 had failed at import on a numpy/numexpr ABI mismatch). That conversion kept the heading structure but not page anchors, and it dropped text, as the next note says.

**Citation style.** `(Ch N, "Section name")`. The conversion this reference was read from did not preserve page anchors, so section names are used in their place. Where a particular point is most clearly attached to a specific subsection (e.g., "What Is Management?"), the subsection heading is used.

**Conversion gaps.** The pymupdf4llm conversion this reference was read from lost a page's text from the start of a feature box: the opening of 110 of the book's 120 feature boxes (Concept Check, Managerial Leadership, Ethics in Practice) was missing, sometimes with the body sentence just before the box (Ch 4.2 lost the end of "allowing time for reentry" with footnote 15, and the "Shaping a Salesperson’s Behavior" feature); a comparison against pdftotext of the original found 1,258 of 17,269 longer lines (7.3%) absent. Ch 12's losses (printed pp. 351, 352, 354, 356: the end of a Ch 12.7 body sentence with footnote 91, the "You Are Now the Leader" feature, the opening of the "Uber’s Need for an Ethical Leader" feature, and two Concept Check items) were restored by hand on 2026-10-15 and Ch 12.7–12.9 read in full. On 2026-10-16 the whole source was re-converted (PyMuPDF text blocks; see the source card). On 2026-10-17 the restored spans were listed by an order-aware word diff of the old and new conversions (runs of 8 or more inserted words), checked against the old text so moved text did not count, and read in full; the Coverage line lists what was added. Table 6.2 (logical fallacies) showed in the diff only because its format changed; its rows were already held and covered. Footnote 46 in Ch 15.5 is present, fused to the next word ("46Culture").

**Coverage scope.** Per Option B in the project's planning log, this deep ref covers the substantive exposition of every chapter — chapter introductions, chapter-overview text, and all numbered substantive sections (e.g., 1.1, 1.2). Six section types per chapter are explicitly excluded as pedagogical scaffolding aimed at undergraduate readers: Key Terms, Summary of Learning Outcomes, Chapter Review Questions, Critical Thinking Case, Management Skills Application Exercises, Managerial Decision Exercises. Appendix A (Theory Building / Scientific Method) is included; Appendix B (Scoring Keys) and the References / Index back-matter are excluded as standard reference apparatus.

**Authorship.** OpenStax flags J. Stewart Black as the lead author via its `display_at_top: true` API field. The book's preface notes that "specialists in a variety of areas have authored individual chapters" — chapter authorship is distributed across the 12 contributors, and the book speaks with multiple authorial voices unified by the OpenStax editorial process. References to "the text" or "the authors" should be understood in this collective sense.

**Licence.** This deep reference describes a CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 source. Direct verbatim quotations from the source carry their `[V]` markers and are attributed to OpenStax via the citation style. Derivatives of CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 source material must be redistributed under the same licence. The distillations derived from this deep reference (aar, decision-making, retro, software-business, stakeholder-engagement) inherit this licence by ShareAlike.

**Spelling.** Verbatim quotations from the OpenStax source preserve American English ("organization", "favor", "behavior"). Paraphrased prose authored for this deep reference uses British spelling per the grounded-forge repo conventions ("organisation", "favour", "behaviour", "analyse").
